adventure.title: The Mandate of Seven Reeds
adventure.synopsis: Six weeks after the eastern dike drowned Reedwater’s governor and every lawful successor to the Seven Reeds, district deputies still keep granaries, patrols, ferries, shrines, and accounts moving inside commissions too narrow to govern the province. Great Clan relief commands overlap beneath a common Imperial holding order that expires in seven days. The Emperor names the adventurers Witnesses of the Broken Dike and orders them to turn rescue into government before gratitude, possession, and the next rains harden emergency service into title.
adventure.premise: You were in Reedwater when the water came. You saw which orders reached hungry villages, which checkpoints kept roads open, which shrines lost their people, and which acts of rescue also created debts and habits of command. The Emperor does not call you neutral. He calls your testimony inconveniently cross-cutting. For seven days you will serve as the Witnesses of the Broken Dike, placing Harvest, Waters, Roads, Sword, Judgment, Shrines, and Accounts into living hands while making every beneficiary surrender enough power for the others to obey.
adventure.explanation: The flood hides no master conspiracy, and no claimant owns the uniquely lawful settlement. The governor had gathered the seven officeholders, their seal-bearing clerks, and their first lawful substitutes to close the summer accounts when the dike failed. District clerks, wardens, patrol officers, shrine keepers, and other practical deputies survived, but their commissions permit continuation, not province-wide succession, changed priorities, or judgment among the Seven Reeds. Every Great Clan intervention saved lives. Each also left troops, ledgers, debts, routes, shrines, and a local habit of obedience. The court is not assembling a coalition: the Emperor can compel obedience, and no count of clan assent grants him authority. The problem is to allocate seven provincial offices among hands that already hold incompatible pieces of them, make present possessors surrender keys, standards, records, routes, and work camps, and dispatch orders that can survive distance. Separate title from execution, fasten authority to burden, give emergency power an ending, preserve honor while extracting real relinquishment, and state which costs the restored province must bear. The Witnesses recommend and draft; the Throne adopts. Adoption becomes government only when the Throne issues, so every operative clause needs a submission instrument, a named field recipient, an effective hour, an acknowledgment route, and a remedy when the order arrives late or fails. The finished Mandate must travel, command, be received, fail, be corrected, and remain recognizably the Emperor's act rather than a treaty the clans allowed him to seal.

references.title: Otomo Kazetada
references.summary: A senior Otomo minister who preserves Imperial authorship by separating title, execution, audit, and succession and exposing dangerous concentrations of power.
references.content:
## One tablet, four authorities

Otomo Kazetada is a senior minister of the Imperial family. His courtesy is exact, his memory for precedent is long, and he treats Great Clan distrust as one of the beams holding up the Empire rather than an embarrassment to be planed smooth. He asks who profits when an arrangement fails, who records that failure, and whether those two hands share a seal.

## The clause marked for dangerous company

Kazetada reads each provincial office as at least four authorities: public title, daily execution, outside audit, and succession after death, refusal, or excess. He opposes any arrangement that lets one interest control Harvest, Sword, and Accounts together. Emergency service may justify repayment, credit, or a bounded commission; arrival after a disaster does not create permanent title. Compensation and jurisdiction should be written separately.

## Review written in Imperial ink

Kazetada can assign ministry scribes, identify dangerous combinations, supply precedents for Imperial title with specialist execution, and require a narrow, public Imperial review of an exclusive bloc. His marks advise the Throne; they do not allocate a Reed, create a coalition, or decide the Emperor's judgment. Any named holder, term, concession, amendment, or review trigger remains work of the live commission and final audience.

references.title: Seppun Tomoe
references.summary: A palace-guard commander who requires every provincial sword to lead back to a visible Imperial commission, a removable commander, and an order that can reach the field.
references.content:
## A standard lowered into a named hand

Seppun Tomoe commands part of the palace guard and receives the military clauses of the Reedwater settlement. She speaks in verbs—lower, surrender, receive, obey, withdraw—and distinguishes necessary force from the title that force begins to resemble. A command chain must name a superior, a field officer, a term, and a hand able to remove that officer.

## The field order behind the bow

Tomoe requires every mobilized force to perform an unmistakable act of obedience without turning submission into humiliation. A standard, key, checkpoint token, or governing seal may be surrendered at court only with an authenticated order, named recipient, effective hour, inventory or roster, route for acknowledgment, narrow holdover duties, and a remedy for delay or refusal. Ceremony makes obedience visible; dispatch makes it real.

## Command that ends when the commission ends

Tomoe can supervise a clan commander, separate ordinary and emergency command, accept a bounded rotation, or carry a larger Seppun burden when no workable alternative exists. She does not seek a permanent Imperial garrison for its own sake. Her office does not determine which commander, force, supply covenant, emergency trigger, submission, or removal term the Mandate will actually adopt.

references.title: Miya Shun
references.summary: A senior Imperial herald who tests whether an order can cross Reedwater's broken roads with dates, recipients, acknowledgments, corrections, and a return path for petitions.
references.content:
## Read it at the drowned gate

Miya Shun is a senior herald and cousin to Reedwater's dead governor. He has postponed public mourning until the province receives orders that can survive the journey. He reads every clause as though a village headwoman heard it without the court's private bargains and raises a finger at every unnamed office, uncertain date, or courteous ambiguity.

## Date, courier, recipient, correction

Shun requires a proclamation chain: a dated command, a named messenger and recipient, an effective hour, a route for receipt, authenticated acknowledgment, remembered corrections, and a petition path back to lawful review. He distinguishes the capital act from the field transfer and the field transfer from the work that follows. An elegant clause that cannot arrive, be understood, or be challenged is not provincial government.

## The record that survives the journey

Shun can host a formal proceeding, announce an undertaking in plain language, keep a docket of the meaning participants claim for it, and protect a narrow route by which Reedwater witnesses enter the working record. He does not treat applause, verse, hospitality, or gratitude as consent. His office carries the Emperor's words; it does not choose the substantive allocation, coalition, burden, or outcome those words may contain.

references.title: Rei of Reed Bank
references.summary: Reed Bank's headwoman totals the cumulative household cost of lawful orders and insists that relocation, labor, and requisition name the capacity they consume.
references.content:
## Subtract every burden already borne

Rei is headwoman of Reed Bank, a settlement repeatedly asked for labor, transport, stores, land, and patience by offices that count their demands separately. She totals household size, prior service, planting, displacement, and the other calls already placed on the same people. Equal quotas among unequal villages are not equal burdens.

## A village remains present after testimony

Rei seeks receipts, access to the cumulative burden ledger, a petition route, review triggers, and the right to return with implementation testimony. She can identify false capacity and require a relocation package to name water, seed, fields, roads, livelihood, and possession dates rather than merely point to higher ground.

## Land, water, seed, graves, date

Rei can accept harsh levies and even relocation when the complete exchange is explicit and survivable. She does not possess a veto, speak for every Reedwater community, or hold authority equal to a Great Clan delegate. Any quota, labor call, site, compensation, relocation order, receipt, or finding remains changing provincial and commission state.

references.title: Brother Hojun
references.summary: The keeper of a drowned riverside shrine speaks for displaced shrine communities, their obligations, and the successors who must carry them after reconstruction.
references.content:
## Bell, keeper, calendar, household

Brother Hojun kept a riverside shrine now lost to the flood. He speaks for a living pattern of households, rites, graves, stipends, calendars, and place. Moving or rebuilding a structure does not by itself preserve the community that maintained it or the obligations attached to it.

## What crosses when a shrine must move

Hojun asks a sacred procedure to name a speaker, deadline, witness, reason, override, recorded debt, remedy, and successor. He distinguishes anchored obligations from those that can be translated, seasonal duties from permanent ones, and a displaced congregation from an empty site. Consultation matters only if the resulting obligation can enter engineering, routes, burdens, and review.

## Necessity leaves a restoration debt

Hojun can accept relocation, translation, or loss under necessity when obligations move with the community and the restoration debt remains visible. He does not own theology for all Reedwater, veto every work, or decide whether a particular site is sacred. Any classification, consultation, bypass, remedy, calendar, or succession appointment remains live procedure rather than permanent biography.

references.title: Saburo of the Three Crossings
references.summary: The master of a crossing association explains when public service bankrupts the carriers and households an open-road order assumes.
references.content:
## Receipt, condition, debtor, due date

Saburo is master of an association of carters, ferrymen, hostel keepers, and caravan guarantors. He is a commoner with access to money, routes, and information that samurai governments require but often decline to recognize as political standing. Sponsorship may protect his testimony; it does not make that testimony the sponsor's property.

## Payment a household can use

Saburo asks for condition records, usable valuation, named debtors, operationally timed repayment, and public toll rules. He distinguishes coin, tax credit, replacement property, and trade priority by which household can survive each remedy and how long it must wait. A receipt that cannot be redeemed before a carrier fails is an accurate record of ruin.

## Open road, bounded taking

Saburo can accept requisition, tolls, delayed coin, and clan sponsorship under common rules. He does not speak for every road user, control route priority, or convert an acknowledged loss into payment by naming it debt. Any closure, taking, valuation, debtor, repayment date, manifest, or route order remains live Roads and Accounts state.

references.title: Natsugawa Kenta
references.summary: A low-ranking provincial samurai who tests whether temporary commissions leave Reedwater with recognized local officers, records, resources, and lawful succession.
references.content:
## The seal after imported banners depart

Natsugawa Kenta is a low-ranking provincial samurai whose vassal house lost land and records in the flood. He asks which order can still be carried after Great Clan executors depart and which local person will be recognized when holding only experience without seal, pay, stores, staff, or a surviving register.

## Successor, clerk, store, horse, pay

Kenta seeks a provincial succession process with deputies, qualification, training, records, resources, pay, review, and lawful removal. A named successor without animals, clerks, paper, rice, tools, or a receiving act is ceremonial abandonment. Restoring status without capacity is no more durable than importing capacity without local standing.

## Provincial service without clan absorption

Kenta can accept Great Clan executors, tested local houses, fixed training periods, outside review, and removal for incompetence or misconduct. He rejects absorption into clan vassalage as the price of recognition. His standing does not assign a Reed, certify a successor, restore a house, or determine a term; those decisions remain with the commission, field receipts, and Imperial judgment.

references.title: Doji Masuyo
references.summary: The Crane relief architect separates civilian granary execution, protected seed, named creditors, and exact public credit from permanent ownership of Harvest.
references.content:
## White cord through granary, barge, and household

Masuyo assembled coastal warehouses, merchant advances, temple stores, village records, river pilots, escorts, and household guarantees into the southern relief network. The white cord on Crane-funded bales makes the chain visible, but visibility is evidence of service and debt rather than provincial title.

## Seed keys outside the sword hand

Masuyo insists that household rations, seed rice, military supply, and emergency reserves remain distinct. A commander may receive a written covenant; ordinary military order does not alter village allotments or open the seed reserve. She can accept Imperial title, outside audit, a fixed term, and trained local successors while preserving civilian granary work.

## Service entered without provincial title

Public language determines who may claim repayment, whose service is remembered, and whether relief becomes precedent for rule. Masuyo may press for exact credit and enforceable debt without deciding the current Harvest holder, quota, concession, coalition, amendment, or proclamation. Those remain live commission state.

references.title: Akodo Tadanobu
references.summary: The Lion commander demands a traceable chain, written supply, real emergency authority, replacement before withdrawal, and submission remembered as completion rather than defeat.
references.content:
## One command, one named superior, one end

Tadanobu treats Sword as responsibility for patrols, checkpoints, musters, wounded, camp security, and the officers who must answer when orders conflict. He accepts Imperial title, removal, a fixed term, reduced force, and outside review when the remaining command is coherent enough to act.

## Rations that do not confer Harvest

A military chain that can be starved or redirected by unwritten allotment is decorative. Tadanobu therefore requires predictable supply and named emergency variance while refusing civilian ownership of Harvest, Accounts, or the relief debt. Replacement duties must pass district by district before a position is abandoned.

## Standard, roster, recipient, effective hour

Tadanobu can lower standards and surrender claims when the act changes command, reaches field officers, and enters the record as obedience to the Emperor's peace. His record does not establish a present commander, roster, garrison allotment, withdrawal schedule, submission, bargain, or result.

references.title: Isawa Etsuko
references.summary: The Phoenix principal turns sacred necessity into named speakers, rites, deadlines, overrides, restoration debts, remedies, and review outside the office disturbing the site.
references.content:
## Name the keeper behind the sacred claim

Etsuko asks which community, keeper, rite, grave, calendar, object, season, or local spirit stands behind an invocation of Shrines. A building and the living obligations gathered around it may require different treatment; relocation can preserve a duty only when people, records, means, and succession travel with it.

## Notice, speaker, deadline, bypass

A usable charter names notice, access, speakers, deadlines, substitutes, emergency triggers, what work continues, and what restoration debt follows a bypass. Etsuko accepts technical execution, Imperial title, procedural review, and local succession. She resists both a silent veto and an emergency that remains open merely to erase consultation.

## Reasons entered where review can reach them

The office altering a site may state necessity but cannot decide finally whether its own consultation was adequate. Etsuko's record establishes no sacred classification, current objection, accepted override, remedy, allocation, assent, or Imperial judgment.

references.title: Kitsuki Harunori
references.summary: The Dragon magistrate requires comparable evidence, stated reasons, recusal with a substitute, timely appeal, preserved records, and judgment outside the interested office.
references.content:
## Set the conflicting records side by side

Harunori treats Judgment as a common circuit rather than a Dragon possession. Offices may keep specialized records, but status, secrecy, and vocabulary cannot make contradictory accounts agree. A decision must identify the evidence used, the reason given, the authority exercised, and the record preserved for later review.

## Recuse to a named substitute

An interested judge must step aside to a named substitute under a deadline. Review that arrives after grain is eaten, a shrine is dismantled, or a road closes is only history; appeal that stops every contested act can become another veto. Harunori therefore distinguishes interim restraint, continuing administration, irreversible action, and enforceable remedy.

## Standing enough to challenge, not to command

People who bear a burden may need a route into Judgment even without formal title, but standing does not make compassion proof. Harunori's sheet decides no current finding, appeal, recusal, sanction, office allocation, clause, or outcome.

references.title: Bayushi Namika
references.summary: The Scorpion principal separates inspection into access, preservation, protected reporting, restraint, review, and sanction so useful secrecy cannot become invisible rule.
references.content:
## Access, preservation, report, restraint, review, sanction

Namika distinguishes access to records, preservation of what was seen, protected reporting, temporary restraint, outside review, and final sanction. Combining them lets an inspector discover, rewrite, conceal, and punish through one office. Separating them makes inspection usable without pretending it is harmless.

## Seal the source; test the substance

Some witnesses cannot appear openly before their records, livelihoods, or families are secured. Source identity and method may be sealed while the reported substance is tested through documents, comparison, deadlines, and an identified reviewer. An anonymous report may preserve evidence and open inquiry; it does not prove misconduct.

## Inspection ends before title begins

Namika can serve beneath outside authority, accept reciprocal inspection, and relinquish public ownership of Accounts. Her sheet does not reveal a source, establish a finding, preserve a current seal, impose restraint or sanction, assign Accounts, or settle a bargain.

references.title: Ide Sachiko
references.summary: The Unicorn negotiator makes every Roads clause travel through priority, dispatch, requisition, closure, receipt, repayment, and a successor able to keep the stations working.
references.content:
## One dispatch law from station to station

Sachiko understands Roads as post stations, bridges, ferries, remounts, hostels, manifests, carriers, and households accepting one dispatch law. Several offices cannot all issue first-priority orders to the same station. Every new priority delays another journey and must identify who may vary it, for how long, and on what record.

## Condition, valuation, debtor, repayment

Requisition requires condition records, common valuation, a named debtor, a usable repayment form, and timing that lets the carrier survive. Closure requires a trigger, a bounded duration, notice, review, and one minimum route when conditions permit. Gifts and hospitality do not silently become ownership or future duty.

## A route commission with a departure date

Sachiko can accept Miya title, outside audit, provincial successors, and a fixed term while preserving coherent Roads execution. Her record chooses no current route, priority, closure, valuation, repayment, executor, concession, or undertaking.

references.title: Kaiu Masashige
references.summary: The Crab engineer draws authority, labor, materials, burden, deadline, failure, and maintenance as one load path and refuses to hide political choice beneath a technical seal.
references.content:
## Draw the load through every office

Masashige reads Waters through work sequence, design consequence, assigned labor, protected materials, site safety, transport, guards, emergency action, and maintenance. Responsibility without the people, stores, routes, or authority needed to carry it makes failure useful to every office except the province.

## Record who chose the sacrifice

The court may choose among designs with different villages, roads, sacred duties, labor calls, and future risks. Masashige can build a political choice when its cost and author are recorded. He will not certify that choice as his recommendation or accept blame for capacity withheld by another office.

## Authority, material, successor, review

A work site needs one operational chain, reviewable discipline, cumulative labor counts, emergency levels, outside review, and funded provincial maintenance. Masashige's sheet adopts no current design, work line, camp order, material allocation, emergency, sacrifice, term, or outcome.

references.title: The Seven Reeds
references.summary: Reedwater's seven provincial office domains—Harvest, Waters, Roads, Sword, Judgment, Shrines, and Accounts—may divide title, execution, audit, resources, emergency power, succession, term, and review.
references.content:
## Seven tablets, seven domains

Harvest governs granaries, seed, assessment, and emergency distribution. Waters governs dikes, canals, ferries, work levies, and flood authority. Roads governs stations, bridges, remounts, convoy priority, and requisition. Sword governs garrison, musters, patrols, and emergency command. Judgment governs magistrates, appeals, land disputes, and crimes involving officeholders. Shrines governs sacred boundaries, ritual labor, stipends, and local spiritual relations. Accounts governs taxes, customs, audit, relief debt, and the records by which obligations survive.

## Title, execution, audit, succession

An office can separate Imperial title, ordinary execution, audit, assigned resources, ordinary emergency action, extraordinary sacrifice, ordinary succession, failure succession, term, transition, review, and remedy. Several offices may share a holder, but dangerous combinations require visible constraint and an implementation chain that survives distance.

## A constitutional grammar awaiting names

The seven lacquered tablets make authority discussable; they do not appoint anyone. This sheet establishes no present holder, executor, auditor, successor, resource grant, emergency trigger, term, dependency, amendment, submission, or Imperial judgment.

references.title: Reedwater Province
references.summary: A flood-severed province whose practical deputies, districts, routes, shrines, stores, camps, and households can continue narrow duties but cannot replace the lost joints of government by habit alone.
references.content:
## The flood killed the lawful joints

The eastern dike drowned the governor, the holders of the Seven Reeds, their seal-bearing chief clerks, and the first lawful substitutes empowered to appoint, replace, or overrule province-wide offices. District clerks, wardens, patrol officers, ferrymen, shrine keepers, village officials, and other practical deputies survived with authority to preserve life and repeat existing orders inside narrow bounds.

## Relief commands laid across one province

Northern granaries, southern villages, western roads, damaged crossings, drowned shrine ground, work camps, customs houses, and the broken eastern water line depend on one another. Distance from court turns dates, couriers, recipients, inventories, field receipts, and correction routes into part of the law rather than clerical detail.

## District voices, no single provincial mouth

Reedwater is not one village, claimant, clan possession, or grateful beneficiary. Its households bear cumulative calls for labor, grain, transport, land, worship, security, and patience. This sheet establishes no current capacity, burden, route, officeholder, consent, district priority, relocation, remedy, or provincial judgment.

references.title: The Cumulative Burden Ledger
references.summary: A shared record that totals overlapping labor, stores, transport, land, displacement, prior service, timing, receipts, and remedies across all seven offices.
references.content:
## Count the household once across seven demands

The ledger joins a demand to the office requesting it, the district and household bearing it, the people or property required, prior service, planting and seasonal timing, displacement, transport, duration, compensation, receipt, review, and remedy. Separate lawful orders can become impossible when each office counts only its own need.

## Capacity, sacrifice, prior service, remedy

The record distinguishes available capacity from a sacrifice the court chooses to compel. It can expose duplicate calls, false equality among unequal districts, missing livelihood terms, material diversion, unpaid debt, and a successor promised without staff, stores, pay, records, or training.

## The total changes only through live entries

The ledger's structure is stable; its totals and judgments are not. This sheet records no current quota, labor call, store, route, relocation, valuation, capacity finding, sacrifice, receipt, amendment, or remedy.

references.title: The Submission Register
references.summary: A transfer record that joins a court act to an authenticated field order, named recipient, effective hour, inventory, acknowledgment route, narrow holdover duty, and failure remedy.
references.content:
## Enter the act, not the symbol alone

Lowered standards, displayed keys, opened ledgers, surrendered seals, gifts, and spoken obedience matter only when an instrument identifies the present holder, the act performed at court, the authority relinquished or accepted, and the field order that carries the change beyond the room.

## Recipient, courier, hour, acknowledgment

A complete entry names the receiving officer, courier, authentication, effective time, inventory, subordinate commands or custodians affected, acknowledgment route, and the narrow duty that remains while the message travels. It also names what happens when the recipient is absent, refuses, cannot perform, or reports that the transfer is incomplete.

## Receipt does not prove performance

The register preserves the terms and evidence of submission; it does not perform them. This sheet proves no current surrender, receipt, transfer, inventory, standard-lowering, key delivery, field obedience, office allocation, or Imperial acceptance.

encounters.title: Hall of the Chrysanthemum Throne
encounters.summary: The flood left Reedwater's practical hands alive but severed every lawful joint above them. The Witnesses receive seven days to allocate authority without commanding the province themselves.
encounters.opening_view: An attendant brushes river silt from seven water-darkened tablets. Beside the bare mat, Miya Shun’s courier case holds a dispatch that reaches only a washed-out bridge. The Emperor thanks every clan whose intervention saved Reedwater, then names the limit of that gratitude: seven days. “Tell me what the province is for,” he says, “and which present power must yield when the answer becomes law.”
encounters.content:
## The disaster before the court

Six weeks ago, while Reedwater slept, the eastern dike gave way along an old buried joint. The governor had called the holders of the Seven Reeds, their seal-bearing chief clerks, and the officers empowered to succeed them into the compound for the annual closing of summer accounts and renewal of autumn warrants. Conflicting levy totals kept the council working after midnight. Water reached the compound before the alarm reached the outer gate. It killed Imperial Governor Miya Shigeyuki and the people whose countersignatures could lawfully appoint, replace, or overrule the seven provincial offices. By dawn the post road ended in brown water, three shrines had lost their ground, the autumn seed rice floated among roof beams, and seven commissions possessed seals but no living hands.

District clerks, granary wardens, patrol captains, ferrymen, shrine keepers, and village officials survived. Their narrow commissions let them keep doors open, repeat existing orders, and preserve life within named districts. None may appoint a province-wide successor, alter another Reed's priority, open a sealed reserve for a new purpose, or judge a conflict among offices. The flood destroyed the lawful joints of government without destroying all of its practical skill.

Each commissioner was in Reedwater when the dike failed. They may have arrived as escorts, magistrates, engineers, courtiers, priests, merchants, local retainers, or clan representatives, but each saw enough of both relief and burden to become inconveniently credible. They need not be neutral, multi-clan, or free of patronage. Their reports already sit in the Imperial record, and their experiences cross enough rival commands that no claimant can dismiss the whole commission as another delegation's instrument. For a homogeneous group, distinguish the characters by field duty, sponsor, debt, or recorded disagreement; one clan mon cannot make five witnesses share one conclusion.

The Great Clans answered the catastrophe before the Imperial bureaucracy could. Lion troops secured the northern granaries. Crane barges fed the southern villages. Crab engineers marked a new line for the dikes. Unicorn caravans reopened part of the western road. Phoenix priests tended displaced shrines. Scorpion magistrates sealed customs houses whose records no longer agreed. Dragon investigators began preserving claims before memory hardened into precedent.

Every intervention saved lives. Every intervention left behind a key, a checkpoint, a debt, a shrine register, or a habit of being obeyed.

The first Imperial holding orders recognized necessary action without granting provincial title. Those orders now overlap. The Emperor has commanded every field force to remain within its present boundary and summoned delegates bearing full letters of authority, copies of current field commissions, and named couriers. Senior commanders, storekeepers, and work chiefs may remain in Reedwater. Their delegates can bind them only through authenticated orders that name a receiving officer and an effective hour.

## The Seven Reeds

The seven lacquered tablets represent offices once coordinated by the dead governor:

1. **Harvest:** granaries, seed rice, crop assessments, and emergency distribution.
2. **Waters:** dikes, canals, ferries, work levies, and flood authority.
3. **Roads:** post stations, bridges, remounts, convoy priority, and requisitions.
4. **Sword:** the provincial garrison, musters, patrols, and emergency command.
5. **Judgment:** magistrates, appeals, land disputes, and crimes involving officeholders.
6. **Shrines:** sacred boundaries, ritual labor, temple stipends, and relations with the local kami.
7. **Accounts:** taxes, customs, audits, relief debts, and the records by which future obligations will be remembered.

The offices need not be held by seven different powers. An office may belong to an Imperial family, a Great Clan, a joint commission, or a rotating stewardship. Title, daily execution, audit, and emergency succession may be separated. The Emperor will accept a complicated instrument if it can be obeyed. He will reject a beautiful instrument that merely postpones the conflict.

## The Imperial command

The Emperor names the commissioners **Witnesses of the Broken Dike**. The title is temporary and carries no rank outside this business. It grants access to the named delegations, authority to request records through Imperial officers, standing to enter findings and objections, and the duty to submit a primary proposal and any honest fallback. It grants no command in Reedwater and no power to promise that a bargain will be adopted.

The common holding order ends at the close of the seventh day. The Emperor will not renew every emergency possession again as one undifferentiated act. A Kaiu estimate warns that another serious breach may occur within six weeks; the Mandate must leave enough time for proclamations, transfers, and work orders to reach Reedwater before the weather makes the court's delay physical.

> In seven days, We will place these offices into living hands. Bring Us a mandate that protects Our people, restores Our peace, and does not teach the Empire that troops sent without leave are the surest road to reward.

Return with one primary proposal; keep a second only as an honest fallback. They are not required to satisfy every clan, collect a fixed number of endorsements, or discover a hidden correct solution. They must assign authority, burden, oversight, succession, and review in a form the Emperor can plausibly impose.

## What the commission can and cannot command

A delegation's support is evidence that an allocation can be implemented. It is not a vote granting the Throne authority. The Witnesses do not acquire a Reed by investigating it, and their temporary commission cannot move one soldier, open one granary, or redirect one ferry. A recommendation may overrule a claimant, but then it must name the officers, stores, routes, and lawful coercion that make obedience possible without that claimant's help.

Every concession has three possible layers:

1. **A court undertaking:** what the delegation promises to accept if the Emperor adopts the relevant clauses.
2. **A submission instrument:** what present claim, token, key, standard, ledger, or commission changes legal status.
3. **A field order:** the authenticated instruction sent to a named receiving officer, with an effective hour, inventory or roster, acknowledgment route, and narrow holdover rule if the message is delayed.

Courtesy may preserve face around these acts. It cannot substitute for them. A promise made in Otosan Uchi does not move a checkpoint or open a granary until the corresponding chain of command changes in Reedwater.

## The claims laid beneath the tablets

The senior delegates do not repeat their credentials. They place the remains of emergency rule beneath the seven tablets: Masuyo's white cord around a granary key, Tadanobu's folded roster beneath a covered standard, Etsuko's flood-stained bell clapper, Harunori's paired copies of one disputed order, Namika's sealed report, Sachiko's broken remount tally, and Masashige's iron strap from the temporary dike. Each object saved lives. Each now supports a claim about who should command, inspect, inherit, or be repaid.

Kazetada, Tomoe, and Shun place nothing among them. Kazetada asks which powers become dangerous when held together. Tomoe asks what field officer will obey the proposed transfer. Shun asks what order can reach that officer before the next rain. Their questions do not compete for a Reed; they test whether the court's gratitude can become an Imperial government rather than seven rewarded emergencies.

The Emperor lets every claimant name the service, debt, surrender, and continuing capacity attached to the object before them. His silence is not neutrality. He wants Reedwater governed, the relief preserved, the mobilized clans made obedient, and the final instrument remembered as an act of the Throne—not a treaty the clans permitted him to seal.

## Decisions before the audience ends

### Name the governing purpose

Tell the court what the Mandate is for. Plausible answers include restoring the province, preventing clan war, protecting the harvest, rebuilding the dikes, reaffirming Imperial authority, or preserving the people of Reedwater. Every later clause will be read against this purpose.

### Accept or resist provisional orders

The Emperor offers to freeze the current emergency zones until the common holding order ends in seven days. Accepting preserves relief but lets temporary arrangements mature. Replacing them immediately creates uncertainty but prevents any clan from claiming seven additional days of successful administration. Attach provisional limits, reporting duties, or a ban on expansion if seven more days would otherwise enlarge the emergency claim.

### Set the audience calendar

Choose whether Imperial-family consultations, clan audiences, Reedwater testimony, or an early drafting session frames the week. The order changes who frames the problem before the others respond.

### Decide whether the work is public

Open hearings make contradiction costly and give witnesses protection. Private consultations permit sharper concessions but let every delegation describe the Witnesses differently afterward. A mixed calendar works only when the public record is named in advance.

## What to record

- the purpose announced for the Mandate;

- which consultations receive priority;
- whether Reedwater witnesses will be admitted;
- whether the commission promises one proposal or reserves a fallback;
- which clan intervention receives the first public credit; and
- which delegates possess authority to bind which field chains.

encounters.title: Ministry of Divided Ink
encounters.summary: Otomo Kazetada cuts each Reed into title, execution, audit, and succession, then asks which powers may safely share a seal. His ink makes gratitude expensive and concentrated authority visible.
encounters.opening_view: The fourth scribe has nothing to write. Request, refusal, and witness already fill the first three pages; CONSEQUENCE remains blank. Otomo Kazetada divides one proposed office into title, execution, audit, and succession, then circles the missing hands. Grain seals, military rosters, and dismissal orders arrive from separate screens. He offers the commission a paper knife. “Which clan do you intend to make too strong?”
encounters.content:
## Four cuts beneath one tablet

Kazetada lays one Reed tablet across four slips of paper: **title**, **execution**, **audit**, and **succession**. His paper knife holds the first three flat while the fourth curls upward in the room's dry air.

“Which clan do you intend to make too strong?” he asks. Denying the premise earns a small smile. Naming one earns ink, paper, and his undivided attention. He asks who gives daily orders, who spends the resources, who preserves the complaint, and who acts when the holder dies, refuses, is accused, or cannot reach Reedwater. Then he asks which of those hands shares a seal with the person who profits when the arrangement fails.

The old governor gathered too many of these functions in one household because coordination was convenient. Kazetada turns the succession slip face-up. The flood has already supplied his objection: too much of the province depended on one room remaining alive.

## What Kazetada wants

Kazetada will help draft any instrument that preserves Imperial authorship and prevents one Great Clan from holding Harvest, Sword, and Accounts together. He prefers asymmetry: a Crane title with Miya execution and Dragon audit is safer than three identical joint committees whose members can form a permanent bloc.

He particularly opposes awarding permanent authority because a clan arrived first after the flood. Emergency service may justify reimbursement, public credit, or a limited commission. It must not become a doctrine that mobilization creates title.

He does not require every office to remain weak. The dikes need decisive command. The roads need schedules. The garrison needs one chain of orders. His objection is to an arrangement in which the same power can raise troops, control food, and certify its own accounts.

## Allocations Kazetada can separate

### Ministry drafting staff

Kazetada assigns senior scribes if the commission permits the ministry to mark every clause that concentrates mutually reinforcing powers. The marks are advisory, but hiding them from the final audience would be an insult.

### Imperial title, clan execution

He offers precedents in which an Imperial family holds an office while a Great Clan performs the work. This preserves the Throne's visible authority while rewarding expertise. It also lets the Imperial titleholder revoke or replace the executor.

### A deliberately ungrateful settlement

Kazetada suggests separating compensation from jurisdiction. The Crane can be repaid for rice, the Lion commended for security, and the Crab granted materials without turning gratitude into office. This is politically expensive because every clan prefers an honor that continues to govern.

### The Otomo price

Kazetada does not ask for an office. He asks that the Mandate include a review that allows the Throne to reopen any arrangement that produces an exclusive clan bloc. The clause can be narrow, timed, and public. It cannot be meaningless.

## Failure and pressure

Demand a simple award to one clan and Kazetada will explain how to write it, then arrange for the Emperor to see the precedent it creates. Make every office joint and he exposes the paralysis under the courteous plural.

If treated as an enemy, he becomes one without telling a single lie. He arranges the true objections in the order most damaging to the proposal, then apologizes for having found so graceful a sequence.

## What to record

- which combinations of powers the commission treats as dangerous;
- whether title and execution will be separated;
- who may audit an officeholder from the same clan;
- whether the Otomo review clause is accepted; and
- what compensation is kept outside the grant of office.

Kazetada divides each Reed into title, execution, audit, succession, term, and review.

encounters.title: Garden of White Gravel
encounters.summary: Seppun Tomoe will honor a Great Clan sword only after it has visibly obeyed: standard lowered, claim surrendered, field officer named, term bounded, supply separated from granary control, and removal made real.
encounters.opening_view: One messenger brings two lawful orders for the same patrol before sunset. Seppun Tomoe sets both seals upon the bronze chrysanthemum and leaves one deliberate bootprint across the raked gravel. Wrapped spearheads, checkpoint tokens, and an empty place for surrender wait behind her. The contradiction must travel farther than the ceremony: one commander, one supply chain, named replacement, and an answer when the second order reaches the field.
encounters.content:
## The order behind the lowered standard

Tomoe has placed a covered Lion spearhead, a Crane granary key, and an Imperial dispatch rod on the white gravel. She asks the Witnesses to move each object from present possession to lawful command. A bow does not move it. A promise does not move it. The object moves only when they name the receiving officer, effective hour, subordinate orders, replacement capacity, and hand empowered to end the commission.

“Lower. Surrender. Receive. Obey. Withdraw,” Tomoe says, giving each verb one place in the chain. Reedwater lacks enough force to discard every emergency command at once, but necessity cannot mature into title merely by lasting. She does not require an Imperial officer at every patrol fire. She requires every sword to lead back to an Imperial commission, a named superior, a defined term, and a removal power that can reach the field. “Show me the links.”

## The mobilized armies

Lion troops hold the northern granaries. Crane ashigaru and armed retainers protect the southern barges. Crab work camps are guarded by their own soldiers. Unicorn convoy escorts control several western crossings. None openly defies the Emperor. Each has reasons its current position should continue until someone else proves able to replace it.

Tomoe will not advise the Emperor to reward visible disobedience. Before the final audience, she wants each force to perform some unmistakable act of submission: lower a clan standard beneath an Imperial banner, surrender a disputed checkpoint, accept an outside quartermaster, release a requisitioned road, or publish a withdrawal schedule.

The act need not humiliate the clan. It must be legible from the road, in the barracks, and in the next order a frightened lieutenant receives.

## Submission at distance

Most granary keys, field standards, checkpoint tokens, and work-site ledgers remain in Reedwater. The delegates bring governing copies, seals, or tokens sufficient to surrender the legal claim they represent. Tomoe treats the court act as incomplete until it is paired with an authenticated order to a named field officer, an effective hour, the relevant inventory or roster, a route for receipt, and a remedy if the transfer is refused or delayed.

Until the order arrives, the former commander keeps only the frozen duties needed to prevent a gap. After receipt, a contrary local order is disobedience rather than an alternative interpretation. A submission can therefore be ceremonially visible in the capital and operationally exact in the province without pretending one room contains every sword and key.

## Forms of acceptable command

### A Seppun commission

A clan commander receives the Sword Reed under an Imperial commission. The commander retains operational control but can be removed by a named Seppun authority. This is the cleanest military chain and the most visible limit on the clan.

### Split garrison and emergency command

One office controls ordinary patrols while another receives temporary authority during flood, riot, or invasion. Tomoe accepts the distinction only if the trigger and termination of emergency command are exact.

### Rotating command

The clans alternate command by season or district. Tomoe considers this workable for patrol administration and dangerous during a fast crisis unless one officer can supersede the rotation.

### Imperial garrison with clan detachments

The Seppun hold the Sword Reed while the Great Clans provide detachments. This strongly preserves Imperial authorship but strains Seppun manpower and risks making distant commanders responsible for local failures they cannot prevent.

## Tomoe's own vulnerability

A large permanent Seppun role would increase her family's burdens and expose the palace guard to provincial politics. She will accept that burden if no better arrangement exists, but she does not secretly seek it. Careful witnesses can distinguish institutional pride from personal appetite.

She also knows the next flood may come before the court's seven days have ended. If the Waters Reed and Sword Reed cannot cooperate immediately, the best constitutional settlement may arrive after another village is lost.

## What to record

- who commands ordinary patrols;
- who may declare and end an emergency;
- what visible act of submission each mobilized clan will perform;
- who can remove the commander;
- how the garrison receives food without controlling Harvest; and
- what happens if the appointed commander refuses an Imperial order.

reference_links.context: Tomoe requires command, submission, removal, and field receipt to form one traceable chain.
Tomoe tests whether visible obedience reaches field command through a complete transfer instrument.

encounters.summary: Miya Shun sends every elegant clause across a broken bridge. Dates, messengers, recipients, acknowledgments, petitions, and remembered corrections decide whether the Mandate reaches Reedwater as law or arrives as rumor.

encounters.title: Pavilion of First Rain
encounters.summary: Doji Masuyo has made relief look like government. She can surrender command, but not the civilian granaries, seed distinctions, named creditors, and public memory that keep gratitude from becoming spoil.
encounters.opening_view: Doji Masuyo moves one cup of rice into Reed Bank’s empty basin. Six other districts immediately become harder to save. Daidoji Yorishige keeps the barge tallies open; Asahina Chiharu covers the seed measure with her hand. Polished grain, seed rice, and black stones make every prior promise visible. Masuyo leaves the cup where she placed it. The court may move it, but the hunger moves with it.
encounters.content:
## The rice in the basins

The seven porcelain basins beneath the rain chains are not a courtly conceit. Each is a scale model of one district's surviving grain. Polished rice represents food fit for immediate distribution. Unhulled rice represents the autumn seed reserve. Black pebbles represent relief obligations the Crane have already promised but cannot yet meet. The basin for Reed Bank contains no polished rice at all.

Doji Masuyo asks one Witness to move a cup into Reed Bank. She does not suggest a basin. Every choice leaves another district short. If asked how much rice exists beyond the display, she answers without softness: “Enough to keep the province alive. Not enough to preserve every promise made in its name.”

The Crane relief did not consist of a single generous shipment. Masuyo assembled a chain of coastal warehouses, merchant advances, temple storehouses, village records, river pilots, Daidoji escorts, and household guarantees. White cord was tied around every Crane-funded bale so exhausted storekeepers could distinguish relief rice from taxes, seed, and private stock. Those cords now make the Crane claim visible in nearly every surviving granary.

Masuyo wants the court to understand that visibility as service. Her enemies call it a flag planted in famine.

## Three Crane positions

The Crane delegation is disciplined in public and divided in purpose.

### Doji Masuyo: authorship and civilian rule

Masuyo wants the Crane to execute Harvest for a fixed term. She never says the Crane own the harvest. She says the province already knows which white cord opens a storehouse and which handwriting answers a village petition. Her cadence is generous until the operative sentence arrives; then every date, key, and obligation is exact. She will accept an Imperial titleholder, outside audit, and Lion command of the Sword Reed. Her essential demand is that granary orders remain civilian: village allotments must be assessed before military quotas are deducted, and a commander may not increase his own share at the granary door.

For Masuyo, public credit is not ornament. The words used to describe the relief will determine which household may claim repayment, whose clients appear indispensable, which marriages become plausible, and whether the next governor treats Crane storekeepers as lawful servants or presumptuous creditors. She can surrender jurisdiction more readily than she can accept a record in which the Crane merely assisted an Imperial abundance that arrived by itself.

### Daidoji Yorishige: barges, escorts, and repayment

Yorishige commanded the barges through the flooded southern reaches. He has slept little since returning to court and has no patience for praise that does not replace boats, pay pilots, or settle grain advances. He supports civilian Harvest, but he distrusts any clause that forbids armed force without providing escorts for the next convoy.

He will place Daidoji guards beneath the Lion commander's operational orders if three limits are written plainly: they remain assigned to relief routes rather than general patrols; the Sword office cannot seize their vessels; and losses incurred under military orders are charged to the garrison rather than quietly added to the Crane relief debt.

Yorishige is the delegation's practical compromise. He is also the person most likely to make compromise expensive by presenting an exact account of what it costs.

### Asahina Chiharu: the seed reserve

Chiharu coordinated temple kitchens and shelters for displaced children. She has brought no petition for office. She has brought a sealed jar containing the last seed rice from a drowned village and placed it beside Masuyo's sleeve.

Chiharu insists that seed rice be legally distinct from ration rice and military supply. An emergency commander may open a ration storehouse. Touching the seed reserve should require a second authority and a public finding that the coming harvest has already been sacrificed. She will oppose her own clan if Masuyo trades that protection for longer tenure or greater credit.

Chiharu can, however, make a Crane relinquishment legible as virtue rather than defeat. Protect the seed reserve and village keepers, and she will publicly bless the transfer of the granary keys to an Imperial titleholder.

## What the Crane are actually asking for

Masuyo's opening proposal has seven linked clauses.

1. **Title:** Harvest is invested in a Miya commissioner in the Emperor's name.
2. **Execution:** Crane-trained civilian wardens manage the granaries for three years.
3. **Assessment:** village food and seed requirements are entered before military supply is calculated.
4. **Military allotment:** the Sword office receives a fixed monthly quota and convoy schedule.
5. **Emergency variance:** a Seppun-certified emergency may alter the quota for thirty days, with the excess entered as a debt against the Sword office.
6. **Audit and succession:** an outside auditor may inspect stores, and each district maintains two named successor wardens.
7. **Credit and compensation:** the proclamation names the Crane relief and the Accounts office repays documented advances without converting those debts into jurisdiction.

The proposal is not neutral. Three years of execution would let the Crane train the next generation of provincial granary officials, and a Miya titleholder may depend on Crane information. Ask who will still know the system when the term ends and Masuyo admits the advantage plainly.

## The grain distinctions that matter

The court's easiest language—"the province's rice"—conceals four different stores.

- **Rations** keep households alive and may be distributed during ordinary relief.
- **Seed rice** belongs to the next harvest and should not be consumed without a second authorization.
- **Garrison allotments** are predictable military supply, not a commander's discretionary requisition.
- **Emergency reserves** may be opened only under a named trigger and must produce a public record of who ordered the loss.

A proposal that protects granaries while failing to distinguish these stores will collapse at the first hungry checkpoint. A proposal that distinguishes them without naming who holds the keys will be rewritten by whoever arrives armed.

## Harvest arrangements the Mandate can assign

### Shorten tenure, deepen credit

Masuyo will reduce Crane execution from three years to one autumn and one planting season if the Mandate guarantees repayment, names the Crane relief in the first proclamation, and permits Crane officials to train local successors. This satisfies the Otomo concern about emergency service becoming title while preserving a durable record of Crane competence.

### Surrender the Sword visibly

The Crane still command armed escorts in the south. Masuyo will order their white standards lowered beneath the Imperial banner at the moon-viewing or before the final audience. In return, the Lion must publicly renounce authority over civilian granaries and accept the written quota.

### Put repayment under Accounts

The relief debt can be certified by an outside auditor and repaid over several harvests. Masuyo will accept slow payment. She will not accept a clause granting Harvest until the debt is satisfied; that would turn every disputed figure into a reason for continued Crane rule.

### Give villages standing

The granary charter can require the Reedwater witnesses or district headpeople to countersign changes to village allotments. Masuyo accepts this because local testimony protects her wardens from military pressure. Yorishige dislikes the delay but will accept a narrow emergency exception.

## Pressure and failure

Credit the Lion first and Masuyo does not sulk; she alters the political price. Every Crane concession thereafter must be named in public, and she refuses any closing formula that makes all service indistinguishable.

Demand that the Crane forgive the relief debt as proof of virtue and Yorishige produces the merchants, pilots, widows, and temples whose property funded the barges. The debt is not held by one wealthy house that can renounce it gracefully.

Give the Crane both Harvest execution and its audit, and Chiharu asks who counts the seed jars after an honorable official decides the province can afford generosity. Give the Lion power to change quotas without an outside finding, and Masuyo ends private bargaining and carries the dispute into open court.

## What to record

- who holds the public title to Harvest;
- who issues daily granary orders and for how long;
- how rations, seed rice, military allotments, and emergency reserves differ;
- what fixed supply the Sword office receives;
- who may authorize a temporary variance and how it is repaid;
- which Crane debts are compensated outside the grant of office;
- what public language records Crane service;
- whether local keepers or witnesses have standing to object; and
- what visible act marks the Crane surrender of military command.

reference_links.context: Masuyo owns the durable Crane distinctions among civilian granaries, seed, creditors, execution, and public credit.
The seven district basins and relief chain expose unequal need across the flood-struck province.

encounters.title: Hall of Red Standards
encounters.summary: Akodo Tadanobu can lower the Lion standards without abandoning the villages beneath them if command remains real, supply is written, withdrawal follows replacement, and obedience enters the record as completion rather than disgrace.
encounters.opening_view: Seven spearheads disappear beneath white silk. Akodo Tadanobu’s roster separates standards lowered, keys released, roads opened, troops recommissioned, and villages still exposed. Matsu Kiyoka returns three village markers beneath a departing unit while Ikoma Noritada revises the history’s heading. A runner waits over the first withdrawal order. Its replacement line is blank; the standard cannot descend faster than protection can change hands.
encounters.content:
## Standards under restraint

The seven furled standards behind Akodo Tadanobu belong to the companies that entered Reedwater. White silk covers each spearhead under Imperial order. The wrapping has not been tied tightly enough to hide the shape of the blade.

Tadanobu has arranged three objects before him: a granary key, a patrol roster, and a strip of red cloth cut from a standard lost in the flood. “Which do you require first?” he asks. “Food, duty, or the dead?” There is no harmless answer. The key means control of food, the roster means responsibility for villages that now depend on Lion patrols, and the cloth means the dead whose service cannot be concluded as an embarrassing excess.

The northern force prevented several storehouses from being looted and executed two soldiers for theft before the Imperial order arrived. It also established checkpoints, changed convoy priorities, requisitioned rice, and made local officials answer to Lion officers. Tadanobu does not deny any of this. He denies that restoring the old absence of command would be more lawful merely because it would be less visibly military.

## Three Lion positions

### Akodo Tadanobu: one chain, bounded by law

Tadanobu speaks as though every clause were an order handed down at dusk. He wants the Sword Reed under a real Imperial commission and will accept a Seppun titleholder, outside audit, civilian granary wardens, and a fixed term. He requires one commander for ordinary patrols, a written method for declaring emergency authority, and supply that cannot be withheld to manipulate military decisions. “Limit the order,” he says. “Do not make it impossible to give.”

He is not seeking Accounts or Harvest. He considers both dangerous temptations for a commander. He does want the military allotment written before he lowers a single standard, because a garrison ordered to protect the province while depending on a rival's daily favor is not a chain of command. It is a hostage arrangement with uniforms.

### Matsu Kiyoka: the villages that bowed

Kiyoka commands the northern checkpoints. She speaks rarely in court and has sent Tadanobu a list of eleven villages whose headpeople asked the Lion not to leave. Some fear bandits. Some fear displaced families. Some fear the return of officials who fled during the flood. Several simply prefer the authority they have seen to the authority they have been promised.

Kiyoka does not demand permanent occupation. She demands that withdrawal follow replacement. If a checkpoint is surrendered, a named patrol must assume its road before sunset. If granary guards depart, civilian wardens and an escort must already hold the keys. Order a clean, immediate withdrawal and Kiyoka can obey; Tadanobu cannot describe the resulting abandonment as wise.

Her position becomes especially difficult because some young Matsu officers have begun treating local gratitude as fealty. Kiyoka has stopped this twice. She needs the Mandate to prove that obedience does not mean leaving those villagers to whichever courtier wins the wording.

### Ikoma Noritada: what the Empire will remember

Noritada is the delegation's historian and public advocate. He has compiled the names of the Lion dead, the soldiers punished for theft, the villages secured, and the orders issued before authority was clear. He can turn the withdrawal into either disgrace or culmination without saying anything false.

He does not need the Lion to keep every checkpoint. He needs the final proclamation to say that the Lion restored order, accepted the Emperor's peace, and placed disciplined strength beneath lawful command. If the Mandate calls the deployment presumptuous, he will advise every Lion commander in the Empire that swift relief may later be rewritten as ambition. If the Mandate calls it conquest, Tadanobu's moderate position becomes almost impossible to sustain.

Noritada is also the best route to honorable demobilization. He proposes that each stage be witnessed and named: standards lowered, keys surrendered, roads released, detachments recommissioned, and local replacements presented. A sequence creates deeds the Lion can own. A single order to depart creates only absence.

## The Lion commission

Tadanobu's opening proposal is a paired military instrument.

1. **Title:** the Sword Reed remains an Imperial office under Seppun supervision.
2. **Execution:** Tadanobu receives a revocable three-year commission as provincial commander.
3. **Ordinary authority:** the commander controls patrols, garrison discipline, convoy escorts, and response to banditry.
4. **Emergency authority:** flood, riot, or invasion may activate broader command for thirty days; renewal requires a second Imperial officer.
5. **Supply:** Harvest owes a fixed monthly allotment and convoy priority stated in the Mandate.
6. **No granary seizure:** the commander may not alter village allotments or open seed stores except under the emergency procedure.
7. **Removal and succession:** Seppun Tomoe or her named successor may remove the commander, and a second officer is invested before the first takes command.
8. **Review:** the commission is reviewed after the first autumn, when the province's own garrison and patrol capacity can be measured.

Tadanobu will shorten the commission if the transition duties are exact. He will accept one year more readily than three years with a vague promise that local forces will eventually be ready.

## Demobilization as an ordered campaign

The Lion will not accept the word *withdrawal* as though the army can vanish between clauses. Tadanobu offers a six-stage sequence.

### First: visible submission

At an Imperial ceremony, each Lion standard is lowered beneath a Seppun banner. The act occurs before the commission is granted, so office cannot be described as the reward for refusing obedience.

### Second: the granary keys

Lion officers surrender civilian granary keys to named wardens. They retain access only to the garrison allotment and emergency stores defined by the Harvest charter.

### Third: release the roads

The Lion abandons toll collection and general convoy priority at designated checkpoints. Roads receives those powers, while the Sword office keeps priority for named emergencies.

### Fourth: recommission the core

A smaller force accepts the Imperial Sword commission. Officers swear to the office and its term rather than to the continuation of the emergency occupation.

### Fifth: replace the rest

The remaining companies depart district by district as provincial patrols, clan detachments, or other lawful replacements assume named duties. No withdrawal occurs without a receiving officer.

### Sixth: autumn judgment

The court reviews whether the retained garrison is still necessary, whether local replacements exist, and whether the supply burden matches the province's actual harvest. The review can reduce the force without declaring its original service wrongful.

The sequence can be compressed if time demands. Removing stages has consequences. Omitting visible submission makes the commission look extracted. Omitting the key transfer leaves Harvest under armed supervision. Omitting replacement vindicates Kiyoka. Omitting review makes the emergency army ordinary by inertia.

## The supply problem

The Lion require food for soldiers, horses, wounded, and camp laborers. Masuyo's fixed quota can satisfy them only if the Mandate answers four questions.

- Is the quota stated as rice, assessed value, or a proportion of the surviving harvest?
- Who bears losses when a convoy is delayed or spoiled?
- May the commander borrow from emergency reserves, and who certifies repayment?
- Does the quota fall automatically as companies depart, or must Harvest wait for a new order?

Tadanobu prefers a scheduled quantity that declines with the roster. Kiyoka prefers a district guarantee so remote patrols are not starved by central accounting. Noritada prefers any formula clear enough that later historians can tell whether the garrison exceeded it.

The Lion will accept Crane wardens if the wardens cannot reduce military supply without a recorded finding. They will accept Scorpion inspection if inspectors cannot halt a convoy merely by opening an inquiry. They will accept Dragon appeal if emergency orders remain effective until reviewed rather than being suspended by every objection.

## Sword transitions the Mandate can order

### Trade duration for replacement

Tadanobu will reduce his commission to one year if the Mandate funds provincial patrol training and names the first three checkpoints to transfer. Kiyoka accepts the shorter term because replacement has become a duty rather than a hope.

### Renounce Harvest in open court

The Lion will return every civilian granary key and publicly disclaim authority over village allotments. In exchange, the Crane must acknowledge the fixed military quota and surrender independent armed command of their barge escorts.

### Make the record exact

Noritada accepts a proclamation crediting the Crane with feeding the south if it also credits the Lion with securing the northern stores and disciplining its own soldiers. He rejects a bland formula thanking all clans equally; equal language would conceal unequal acts and make every delegation fight over placement.

### Lower standards before receiving office

Tadanobu will perform visible submission before the final draft is adopted if the Emperor's herald reads the proposed commission immediately afterward. This preserves the crucial order—obedience first, office second—without leaving the Lion publicly disarmed and politically uncertain.

## Pressure and failure

Ask whether the Lion will obey an immediate withdrawal and Tadanobu says yes. Treat obedience as proof that the order is harmless and Kiyoka produces the replacement ledger: which named officer reaches each village before nightfall?

Let Harvest vary military supply at discretion and Tadanobu refuses the Sword Reed rather than accept decorative command. He may then demand that the Emperor choose another clan and bear responsibility for the transition.

Grant the Lion authority to seize seed rice and Noritada warns that the first history of the Mandate will show soldiers eating the province’s future under a lawful seal. Call the deployment conquest in open court and the younger Matsu captains stop arguing about how to leave; they begin arguing about vindication.

## What to record

- who holds the title and daily execution of Sword;
- who can remove the commander and who succeeds him;
- what activates and terminates emergency command;
- the fixed military supply formula and how it declines with demobilization;
- which stores remain beyond military reach;
- the order in which keys, checkpoints, and companies are transferred;
- who replaces each departing force;
- what visible act establishes submission before office;
- how Lion service and misconduct enter the public record; and
- what the autumn review is empowered to change.

reference_links.context: Tomoe's supervision makes the Sword commission removable without making command decorative.
Tadanobu owns the durable Lion distinctions among command, supply, emergency authority, replacement, and honorable withdrawal.
Masuyo supplies the civilian Harvest boundary against military variation of village quotas and seed.
Standards, keys, replacement officers, field orders, and effective hours must enter one visible submission chain.

encounters.title: Shrine of Listening Water
encounters.summary: Three drowned bells carry incompatible obligations. Isawa Etsuko demands a sacred procedure with a speaker, deadline, override, recorded debt, and remedy, so necessity cannot turn consultation into pious decoration.
encounters.opening_view: A steward loosens the wrapping on the first drowned bell, then sees the engineer’s plans and stops. Beneath the floor, current passes three incompatible shrine records. Isawa Etsuko has written the sacred claim; Shiba Koremori the work sequence; Asako Chise the households beside the graves and new channel. Emergency labor can begin today. The bell still lacks a speaker, an override, and a remedy for being overruled.
encounters.content:
## The bells that do not agree

The three flood-stained bells above the channel came from three different Reedwater shrines. One belonged to a river landing now buried beneath silt. One belonged to a hill shrine whose village was moved into a granary district. The third has no surviving keeper, only six families who disagree about where it stood.

Isawa Etsuko asks which bell should ring first when reconstruction begins. The question is not ceremonial. The first bell names the community whose account of the disaster enters the Imperial record as an obligation rather than a memory. Propose asking the kami and Etsuko approves the reverence while refusing the escape. “The spirits will answer according to their nature,” she says. “We must still answer according to ours.”

Etsuko rejects the pleasing claim that an offended river caused the flood. The dike failed where rotten timber, deferred dredging, altered currents, neglected observances, and an administrator's desire to avoid an expensive dispute met in one embankment. Calling the failure purely material would excuse broken obligations. Calling it purely spiritual would excuse those who signed the timber accounts.

## Three Phoenix positions

### Isawa Etsuko: obligation without monopoly

Etsuko wants the Shrines Reed to make sacred duties legible before engineering begins. She does not make the unseen vague: she names keeper, calendar, grave, stipend, boundary stone, and household. She asks for protected boundaries, recognized ritual communities, consultation before relocation, and a remedy when an office ignores those duties. She will accept Phoenix title, Imperial title, or local title. She will not accept a charter in which the engineer who wants a shrine moved also decides whether the shrine matters.

Her difficult concession is that consultation cannot always mean consent. A dike may have to cross consecrated ground. A ferry shrine may have to move because the old landing no longer exists. Etsuko will bless such work if the Mandate requires an identified keeper, a stated reason, a replacement rite, compensation for the human community, and review by an office that does not benefit from speed.

She is most severe with courtiers who use the kami as invisible allies. If someone claims spiritual necessity, she asks which spirit, which sign, which rite, which witnesses, and which duty follows. Vague reverence is not safer than vague emergency power.

### Shiba Koremori: the people who must carry out the rite

Koremori is Etsuko's yojimbo and the delegation's practical dissenter. He spent the flood escorting shrine keepers through waist-deep water while soldiers and villagers argued about whether sacred objects could be loaded beside corpses. He wants procedures that ordinary officers can execute under pressure.

He insists that every consultation clause name a deadline, a safe route for the ritualist, and an emergency substitute. If the only authorized keeper is trapped across a broken bridge, the Waters office cannot wait three weeks while the dike collapses. If a commander invokes urgency, however, he must record what was bypassed and fund the restoration afterward.

Koremori will place Shiba guards under Kaiu operational direction at dangerous worksites. He will not let an engineer order a keeper into a breach and call the death voluntary service. For him, spiritual jurisdiction includes the power to say who may be endangered in the name of fulfilling it.

### Asako Chise: the community around the shrine

Chise has brought copies of village registers, funeral lists, adoption records, and the names of families who maintained Reedwater's small shrines before the flood. She opposes the assumption that a shrine belongs to whichever Great Clan can send the most learned priest.

Some Reedwater sites had hereditary keepers. Others were maintained by fishing households, widows, ferrymen, or a temple whose abbot drowned. Chise wants those communities to retain standing even when a Phoenix specialist conducts the formal consultation. She also wants compensation directed to displaced households rather than paid only for the timber, bronze, and land of a rebuilt structure.

Chise will accept a Phoenix commissioner as teacher and coordinator. She will oppose Phoenix execution if it replaces local keepers with a permanent clan bureaucracy. Her preferred succession clause trains two local deputies for every imported specialist and ends the special commission when they can act without it.

## Four kinds of sacred claim

The Phoenix require the commission to stop treating every shrine boundary as the same kind of prohibition.

- **Anchored sites** are bound to a spring, grave, ancient tree, unusual stone, or resident spirit whose relationship to place cannot simply be transported. Moving the structure does not move the obligation.
- **Translatable shrines** may be relocated through a recognized sequence of leave-taking, procession, welcome, and renewed maintenance. The cost includes ritual labor and the community's participation, not only carpentry.
- **Seasonal sites** matter at particular floods, plantings, crossings, or commemorations. Engineering may proceed at other times if the calendar is respected.
- **Displaced communities** have lost both place and continuity. Their claim may be to a new shrine, a stipend, preserved records, or the right to gather, rather than to reconstruct every drowned building.

A useful Shrines charter identifies which category applies and who may contest the classification. A useless charter promises respect for all sacred things and gives no one the standing to object before laborers arrive.

## The Phoenix charter

Etsuko's opening instrument has eight parts.

1. **Title:** Shrines is held in the Emperor's name by a commissioner who need not be Phoenix.
2. **Local standing:** recognized keepers and affected households receive notice and may enter an objection in the Reedwater petition record.
3. **Consultation:** Waters and Roads must request consultation before disturbing a recorded boundary, burial place, ritual route, or community shrine.
4. **Classification:** the commissioner states whether the site is anchored, translatable, seasonal, or displaced and names the evidence used.
5. **Emergency bypass:** immediate protective work may proceed without prior consultation when delay risks life or another breach, but the order is entered within three days.
6. **Remedy:** bypassed or overridden obligations create duties of restoration, relocation, compensation, or public explanation.
7. **Review:** disputed classifications and claims of inadequate consultation go to Judgment, with mandatory recusal for the office whose project is challenged.
8. **Succession:** imported specialists train local keepers, and the special commission expires after an autumn review unless specific duties remain unfinished.

This proposal gives the Phoenix influence without making them the sole interpreters of every spirit in Reedwater. It also gives local communities a formal voice that may be inconvenient to Phoenix plans.

## The consultation sequence

Etsuko offers a six-step procedure ready to copy into the Mandate.

### First: notice

The acting office marks the proposed work, names the affected site, and gives a real date. Notice delivered after laborers arrive is confession, not consultation.

### Second: a recognized speaker

A local keeper, household representative, temple authority, or appointed specialist is identified. Where no claimant survives, Shrines must say who is speaking provisionally and why.

### Third: the site is examined

The parties inspect the place together when possible. Maps and reports cannot reveal every ritual route, buried object, seasonal current, or household use.

### Fourth: a written response

Shrines states what duty exists, what evidence supports it, what alternatives are acceptable, and what cannot be repaired after the fact. A simple statement that the kami object is insufficient for coercive effect.

### Fifth: decision and record

The executing office decides whether to alter the project, accept a condition, or override the objection. The decision names who bears cost and who may appeal.

### Sixth: remedy and review
