If a duty was bypassed, the promised restoration occurs on a date. Judgment may review whether consultation was real; it does not replace the spiritual finding with its own theology.

## Sacred procedures the Mandate can authorize

### Phoenix title, Kaiu execution

Etsuko will accept Kaiu control of the Waters work if Shrines has prior notice, site access, and an appeal path. Masashige gains clear engineering command. The Phoenix gain no power to direct labor merely by objecting.

### Imperial title, local succession

A Miya or Otomo commissioner can hold Shrines while Etsuko trains local deputies. Chise strongly supports this form if village keepers receive stipends and standing. The Phoenix receive less durable jurisdiction but more credible proof that the commission serves Reedwater rather than clan expansion.

### Emergency work with a spiritual debt

Koremori will accept a broad emergency bypass if it expires quickly and automatically creates a recorded duty of restoration. The office cannot erase the debt by later declaring that the emergency proved consultation unnecessary.

### One review forum for material and sacred disputes

Harunori's circuit can hear whether notice, recusal, and remedy were lawful without deciding whether a spirit truly spoke. Etsuko accepts this boundary. She rejects a tribunal that treats spiritual testimony as valid only when accompanied by evidence a magistrate personally understands.

## Pressure and failure

Give Shrines an absolute veto and Etsuko asks who reviews a Phoenix claim that happens to protect Phoenix influence. If they answer no one, she warns that reverence has been converted into office without confession.

Make consultation advisory and consequence-free and Chise reads the names of three drowned communities whose administrators also promised to listen. The difference between courtesy and jurisdiction is whether ignoring the answer creates a duty.

Let emergency authority erase sacred claims permanently and Koremori asks why any office would ever finish declaring an emergency. If they require unanimous local consent for every alteration, he asks which dike should fail while six displaced families dispute who inherited a bell.

Ask the Phoenix to certify the moral purity of the whole Mandate and Etsuko refuses. A blessing can witness duties undertaken. It cannot make an incoherent instrument safe.

## What to record

- who holds the public title and daily execution of Shrines;
- which local keepers and communities have standing;
- what sites require notice and how they are classified;
- who may speak provisionally when no keeper survives;
- what a consultation must state to constrain another office;
- when emergency work may bypass consultation;
- what restoration, relocation, compensation, or explanation follows;
- who reviews procedure and which judges must recuse;
- how imported specialists train local successors; and
- which bell, community, or duty is named first in the opening rites.

reference_links.context: Hojun's displaced community tests whether sacred consultation preserves people as well as sites.
Etsuko owns the consultation grammar of named speakers, deadlines, override, restoration debt, and review.
Harunori supplies outside procedural review without claiming authority to decide theology.
Masashige supplies the technical execution boundary when work disturbs a sacred site.
The drowned and displaced communities belong to provincial continuity rather than one building or clan office.

encounters.title: Stone-and-Moss Court
encounters.summary: Kitsuki Harunori turns the clean face of law into the earth. Judgment must reach evidence, recuse without vanishing, permit urgent action, preserve appeal, and remain an Imperial circuit rather than Dragon possession.
encounters.opening_view: Kitsuki Harunori turns the central stone, hiding its clean face against the earth. An emergency order waits with Mirumoto Daizen; Togashi Sorin brings a claimant the ordinary rules cannot seat. Between them lies an accused official’s unopened seal. Harunori removes the first judge’s name from the circuit and sets out recusal, substitute jurisdiction, interim protection, appeal, and remedy. Dusk will not recuse itself.
encounters.content:
## The stone turned over

The clean central stone has not been scrubbed. Harunori turned it over before the Witnesses arrived. Its hidden side bears the stains of years beneath the soil, while the surface everyone remembers is now face-down.

He places seven wooden tablets around it, one for each Reed, and asks for a magistrate beside every office. Whenever they name a judge from the clan holding title, execution, or audit, Harunori moves that judge onto the central stone. Soon the clean face is crowded. “Remarkable,” he says. “Impartiality appears to require a very large stone.”

This is his argument without accusation: every delegation supports impartial law until impartiality requires someone else to judge its own necessity. The Mandate can divide offices carefully and still fail if every dispute returns to the power whose conduct produced it.

Harunori does not ask for permanent Dragon possession of Judgment. He prefers an object to an accusation and a question to a conclusion. He asks what record exists, whose hand can alter it, what standard governs the decision, and what happens while review is pending. His politeness gives people time to notice that they have placed themselves on the overturned stone. What he asks them to build is a circuit that survives the first recusal, missing magistrate, emergency order, and petitioner too low in status to be heard conveniently.

## Three Dragon positions

### Kitsuki Harunori: evidence and stated reasons

Harunori wants Judgment to preserve records, identify conflicts of interest, and require reasons that can be compared with what actually occurred. He knows the Kitsuki method is regarded by many courts as graceless at best and presumptuous at worst. He does not propose to replace testimony, status, oath, and reputation with a footprint held up triumphantly before a daimyo.

He does insist that rank cannot make two contradictory granary ledgers agree, that a sealed order cannot authorize an act dated before it was written, and that a magistrate should not call a conclusion inevitable when the record preserves alternatives. Evidence is not a weapon against etiquette. It is a restraint on convenient memory.

Harunori will accept Imperial title, rotating clan magistrates, or a mixed circuit. He requires preserved reasons, access to records, and automatic recusal where a judge's clan materially benefits from the office under review.

### Mirumoto Daizen: a judgment that arrives in time

Daizen commands the small Dragon escort and has served as an enforcing magistrate. He distrusts procedures designed by people who never had to carry an order to armed officers before dusk.

He wants every appeal path to have a substitute judge and a deadline. Recusal without replacement allows a powerful respondent to disable the forum by implicating every available magistrate. Appeal without interim authority lets each office suspend an unwelcome order by filing a petition. Retrospective review without a remedy becomes a history lesson delivered to the injured.

Daizen supports immediate emergency orders that remain effective during review, but only for a short stated term. He also wants Judgment to possess a narrow power to preserve records, seal disputed stores, or stay an irreversible act. It should not take command of a dike or garrison merely because litigation exists.

### Togashi Sorin: the claimant law does not expect

Sorin is a monk whose travel-stained robe makes him easy to mistake for an attendant until he speaks. He asks what happens when the right claimant is a ferryman's widow, a displaced keeper, a child adopted after the flood, or a village whose surviving headman owes his office to the commander it must accuse.

He does not oppose Harunori's evidence. He opposes the belief that a complete record exists before someone has been allowed to speak. Sorin wants standing rules broad enough to admit those who bear a duty or burden even when they hold no title to the disputed office or land.

He also asks what Judgment is for. Punishment may be required, but many Reedwater disputes need restored grain, rebuilt access, replacement labor, a corrected proclamation, or a new official—not merely a declaration that the former official acted wrongly. Sorin presses the Dragon toward remedies that repair relationships rather than perfecting the court's account of failure.

## The common circuit

Harunori proposes a Judgment structure with four layers.

1. **Local petition officers** receive complaints, preserve initial records, and can order a brief pause when an irreversible act is imminent.
2. **A three-seat provincial circuit** hears disputes among Reeds, claims against officeholders, and appeals from local petition officers. One seat is Imperial; the other two rotate among clans not materially interested in the dispute.
3. **An emergency reviewer** examines extraordinary orders after they take effect. Review does not automatically suspend the order, but it can terminate renewal, require compensation, or refer misconduct.
4. **An autumn panel** reviews patterns rather than isolated cases: repeated recusals, missing records, unpaid remedies, and offices that invoke emergency authority as ordinary practice.

Judgment is not the auditor, prosecutor, commander, or shrine authority. It decides whether those offices used their own powers lawfully and whether promised remedies occurred.

## Recusal as a chain, not an absence

The Dragon delegation offers a sequence for every contested office.

### Disclosure

A magistrate states the clan, household, debt, kinship, command, or office relationship that may affect judgment. Secret conflicts discovered later are treated more severely than disclosed conflicts managed openly.

### Decision

Some conflicts require automatic recusal: the judge's clan holds the office under review; the judge helped issue the disputed order; the judge or household has a direct relief debt; or the judge would review an inspector the judge appointed and may dismiss.

Other conflicts may be waived by all parties or reviewed by the Imperial seat. Not every acquaintance empties the court.

### Substitute jurisdiction

The charter names who acts next. A first substitute and a failure substitute are appointed before the office begins work. A recused magistrate may preserve records and prevent immediate destruction but may not decide the merits.

### Deadline

The substitute accepts or declines the case promptly. If the deadline expires, jurisdiction passes automatically rather than waiting for a fresh favor from court.

### Interim order

The circuit states what remains in force while review proceeds. Reversible administration usually continues. Irreversible destruction, transfer, execution, or dispersal may be paused narrowly.

### Recorded reason

The recusal, substitute, deadline, and interim order enter the public procedural ledger even when evidence or witness names remain sealed.

Without these steps, recusal becomes either a fiction or a veto. With them, a clan can surrender judgment over itself without surrendering access to law.

## Evidence, testimony, and records

Harunori identifies five records the Mandate must preserve across all Reeds.

- the order as issued, including date and seal;
- the office's stated ground for acting;
- the material record used, such as manifests, maps, rosters, shrine registers, or grain counts;
- objections and consultations received before action when time allowed; and
- the result, including costs, injuries, transfers, and promised remedies.

Witness identities may be sealed. Military routes may be summarized. Sacred materials may be restricted to qualified readers. The existence of a record, the office holding it, and the date it must become reviewable cannot remain secret indefinitely.

Harunori refuses a Mandate in which every office keeps its own archive in a different vocabulary. He supports Miya copies and Scorpion comparison because common law requires records that can meet each other.

## Judgment circuits the Mandate can establish

### Dragon execution, Imperial title

A Seppun or Otomo titleholder may appoint Harunori to organize the circuit for one year. The Dragon receive no permanent claim, and local or mixed successors must be trained before autumn review.

### Rotating seats with fixed recusals

Each Great Clan may name qualified magistrates, but automatic conflicts are written in advance. This reduces the appearance of Dragon tutelage while preserving the circuit's structure. Daizen insists on preselected substitutes so rotation does not become vacancy.

### Emergency action, retrospective teeth

Sword and Waters may act immediately under defined triggers. Judgment cannot halt necessary action merely because an appeal is filed. It can end renewal, compel restitution, remove an official through the titleholder, and publish repeated misuse at autumn review.

### Protected petitioners, tested accusations

Namika can provide confidential reporting channels; Sorin supports broad standing; Harunori requires corroboration before sanction. The combination protects witnesses without making anonymous accusation itself a judgment.

## Pressure and failure

Give Judgment power to suspend every contested order and Daizen asks how many objections a rival needs to stop a convoy. If they deny all interim power, Harunori asks what appeal remains after a shrine is dismantled, a seed store consumed, or a witness removed.

Require recusal without a substitute and Sorin quietly identifies relationships until every magistrate is disqualified. The exercise is not mockery. It demonstrates how easily purity can abolish jurisdiction.

Give the Dragon permanent Judgment and Harunori asks whether future Dragon offices will still be judged by Dragon magistrates. If the answer is yes, the principle has failed. If the answer is no, permanent Dragon title is unnecessary.

Treat low-status testimony as beneath the court and Sorin asks whether the Mandate governs only those permitted to enter it. If they accept every claim without testing, he asks whether compassion has become a method by which the most practiced liar acquires a village's labor.

## What to record

- who holds title and execution of Judgment;
- who may petition and what burdens create standing;
- which conflicts require automatic recusal;
- who acts as first and failure substitute;
- how quickly jurisdiction transfers;
- what remains effective during appeal;
- which irreversible acts may be paused;
- what records every Reed must preserve;
- which witness identities or materials may remain sealed and for how long;
- what remedies Judgment may order or recommend; and
- how the autumn panel detects patterns no single case reveals.

reference_links.context: Kenta's succession concern tests whether Judgment remains reachable after temporary officers leave.
Harunori owns the common circuit, preserved reasons, recusal, substitute jurisdiction, appeal, and remedy.
Namika supplies the inspection and secrecy questions Judgment must review without absorbing Accounts.

encounters.title: Theater of a Thousand Sleeves
encounters.summary: Seven empty robes accuse an absent eighth. Bayushi Namika divides inspection into access, preservation, protected reporting, restraint, review, and sanction, exposing where secrecy shelters truth and where it shelters power.
encounters.opening_view: Seven empty robes perform accusation without an accused. A screened witness withholds a public name; Shosuro Mirei catches the message that slips beneath the curtain. Soshi Kureha places two identically sealed customs copies side by side—their totals disagree. Bayushi Namika watches the audience as the accusing sleeve halts above the open ledger. Truth has reached the stage; publication, protection, inspection, and sanction have not yet agreed on an entrance.
encounters.content:
## The actors with no bodies

The seven robes on the empty stage move through a short play before Namika speaks. Harvest receives a sealed bale. Sword demands it. Roads diverts it. Waters claims the boat. Shrines covers the seal with a prayer strip. Judgment asks for the original order. Accounts enters six different explanations in six different ledgers.

At the end, every sleeve points toward an absent eighth figure. No robe represents that person.

Namika asks whether the missing figure is a thief, a witness, an auditor, or the Emperor. Whatever answer the Witnesses give, she praises the choice and asks who profits from the other three absences. The answer changes with the viewer. That is the point.

The Scorpion did not create that failure. They are unusually well equipped to exploit it. Namika offers the same skills as remedy and waits for the commission to admit why remedy and danger resemble each other.

## Three Scorpion positions

### Bayushi Namika: authority that survives public suspicion

Namika speaks as though every accusation were a gift whose wrapping deserves admiration. “A title would only make people suspicious,” she says, pausing just long enough to acknowledge the joke. She wants access to manifests, the right to compare records across offices, a protected route for reporting discrepancies, and a guarantee that an inspected official cannot dismiss the inspector. She prefers a narrow office whose usefulness is harder to deny and whose limits are plain enough that rivals can accept it.

She will serve under Otomo, Miya, or mixed Imperial authority. She will accept Dragon review and reciprocal inspection. She refuses an arrangement in which her findings may be ignored privately whenever they embarrass a favored clan.

Namika's public concession is powerful: the Scorpion can relinquish Accounts title before the court, allowing other clans to support their involvement without confessing trust. Her private demand is that the relinquishment not reduce inspection to an invitation.

### Shosuro Mirei: the witness who cannot appear

Mirei directs the theater and has spoken only through actors during the first half of the meeting. She coordinated observers at Reedwater's docks, storehouses, and checkpoints. Some are samurai. Some are clerks, boatmen, servants, merchants, or people whose testimony would expose a disobedient superior.

She wants protected reporting that separates the identity of a source from the substance that can be tested. An inspector may know the name. The preliminary report may use a cipher. A reviewing magistrate may examine the sealed identity if credibility becomes decisive. The inspected office does not receive a list of everyone who spoke before safeguards exist.

Mirei is not asking the Mandate to treat rumor as proof. She wants a route by which a frightened person can cause records to be preserved before the official controlling those records learns whom to punish.

### Soshi Kureha: seals, copies, and custody

Kureha maintains the Scorpion's duplicate manifests. She is less interested in secrets than in the physical life of a record: who wrote it, who sealed it, who copied it, when it changed hands, and which version appeared after an inquiry began.

She wants inspectors to copy or seal records they examine. Access without custody lets an office display one ledger today and replace it tomorrow. Custody without an index lets inspectors remove papers and later claim they never existed. Kureha proposes numbered copies, witnessed seals, and a register held outside Accounts.

She opposes giving Scorpion inspectors the power to impose punishment. The same person should not collect the source, interpret the discrepancy, decide whether secrecy is justified, and sanction the accused. Her caution is institutional rather than moral: an office that performs all four functions will eventually produce the conclusions its patrons reward.

## The six powers hidden inside inspection

Namika requires the word *inspect* to be divided before it is assigned.

1. **Access:** enter a storehouse, checkpoint, office, or archive and see the relevant record.
2. **Comparison:** match manifests, seals, dates, quantities, routes, and orders across Reeds.
3. **Preservation:** copy, index, or seal a record so later review concerns the same evidence.
4. **Protected reporting:** convey a discrepancy to an authority that cannot be blocked by the inspected office.
5. **Interim restraint:** briefly halt destruction, transfer, or disappearance while Judgment acts.
6. **Sanction:** punish misconduct, recover goods, remove an official, or alter an office.

The Scorpion seek the first four and a very narrow version of the fifth. They do not need the sixth. Judgment can decide sanction; titleholders can remove; Harvest or customs authorities can recover goods. This division makes Scorpion expertise useful without giving the clan a private government made of ledgers.

## What happened to the customs record

The surviving Reedwater books contain at least five incompatible exemptions.

- Lion checkpoints waved through military supply under emergency orders.
- Crane barges treated relief cargo as outside ordinary customs.
- Unicorn caravans recorded feed and remount exchanges by route rather than by district.
- Crab engineers requisitioned timber and stone against future Imperial compensation.
- Shrine and temple stores moved goods under seals that local collectors hesitated to open.

None of these practices proves theft. Together they make theft, favoritism, duplication, and honest error almost impossible to distinguish after the fact. Namika can identify where quantities fail to reconcile. She cannot decide alone which necessity justified the discrepancy.

Decide whether Accounts is chiefly a tax office, audit office, customs archive, relief-debt registry, or institutional memory. One office may perform all these tasks only if their internal powers are divided.

## The secrecy ladder

Mirei offers five levels rather than a single choice between public and secret.

### Public rule

The mandate, inspection scope, record categories, reporting authority, recusal rules, and maximum periods of secrecy are public. No one should discover the inspector's powers only after being inspected.

### Confidential source

A witness identity may remain known only to the receiving inspector and a named reviewing authority. The substance must be recorded precisely enough to test without exposing the source automatically.

### Sealed interim finding

A preliminary discrepancy may remain sealed while records are preserved and retaliation risks are assessed. The sealed report has a date, custodian, and deadline.

### Reviewable finding

Judgment, Otomo, or another named authority receives the evidence and can test the inspector's method, conflicts, and conclusions. The inspector cannot convert source protection into immunity from review.

### Public disposition

The final disposition states what category of problem occurred, what remedy followed, and what office was responsible. Names or methods may remain protected where necessary, but authority cannot rest forever on an unseen conclusion.

Secrecy without a ladder becomes permanent convenience. Publicity without stages destroys the people and methods that make inspection possible.

## The inspection sequence

Namika's proposed office acts in seven steps.

1. A discrepancy, complaint, or scheduled audit opens a numbered inquiry.
2. Inspectors identify the records and sites within scope; expansion requires a recorded reason.
3. Copies or seals preserve the evidence, with a duplicate index outside Accounts.
4. Witness information is separated into testable substance and protected identity.
5. A preliminary report distinguishes error, unresolved discrepancy, plausible necessity, and suspected misconduct.
6. Judgment or the titleholder decides restraint, recovery, sanction, or closure, subject to recusal.
7. A final disposition enters the common record, and sealed materials receive a later review date.

An inspector may briefly preserve a ledger, cargo, or seal from destruction. An inspector may not stop a grain convoy indefinitely merely by opening an inquiry. Daizen's deadlines and Harunori's substitute jurisdiction make the limit real.

## Inspection powers the Mandate can divide

### Relinquish Accounts title, retain inspection

Namika will publicly support an Imperial or Miya titleholder if Scorpion inspectors receive statutory access, preserved reporting, and outside dismissal. This is the cleanest visible relinquishment in the triangle.

### Reciprocal inspection

The Scorpion accept inspection of their own records, source-handling procedures, and expenses by a Dragon or Otomo reviewer. Witness identities remain sealed unless the reviewer finds a stated reason to open them. Kureha supports this because chain of custody should constrain inspectors first.

### Customs access for bounded Roads

The Unicorn may administer crossings and tolls if manifests use a common form and inspectors may compare them without seizing routine cargo. The Scorpion gain information; the Unicorn gain protection against later accusations based on incomparable books.

### A public performance instead of a public confession

Mirei can stage the sequence of emergency exemptions so every delegation admits its own exception without being singled out as corrupt. The performance creates consent for common records. Individual misconduct found later remains answerable.

## Pressure and failure

Give the Scorpion title, inspection, custody, secret reporting, and sanction, and Namika asks who will inspect her. “The Scorpion” ends the lesson. “No one” proves the court wants an instrument of fear rather than Accounts.

Make every source public and Mirei removes three reports, asking whether the court prefers incomplete truth delivered honorably. If they accept every sealed accusation as fact, she replaces one actor's script with another and asks which unseen author they just empowered.

Allow the inspected office to dismiss inspectors and Kureha returns a ledger to its owner, then asks the Witnesses to remember its contents. If inspectors may seize records without an index or witness, she asks why the court should trust the copy more than the original.

Exclude the Scorpion because their expertise is dangerous and Namika agrees—then asks which safer delegation can compare the books before the final audience. Refusal is a choice to leave the problem with those who benefit from it.

## What to record

- who holds title and daily execution of Accounts;
- which inspection powers are granted separately;
- which records and sites inspectors may access;
- how copies, seals, and custody are witnessed;
- who may dismiss an inspector and for what cause;
- how witnesses report without making rumor dispositive;
- how long preliminary findings may remain sealed;
- which authority reviews methods, conflicts, and conclusions;
- what narrow interim restraint inspectors possess;
- who decides recovery, sanction, and removal;
- what final disposition becomes public; and
- who inspects the inspectors.

reference_links.context: Namika divides inspection into access, preservation, reporting, restraint, review, and sanction.
Harunori supplies the outside reviewer, stated reasons, and appeal boundary that keep secrecy from ruling alone.

encounters.title: Courtyard of Bells
encounters.summary: Every bell marks a road, a delay, or a taking. Ide Sachiko can make Reedwater move if priority is singular, requisition becomes valued debt, closures preserve one minimum route, and households survive the map drawn across them.
encounters.opening_view: Four bells announce four claims upon one road: remount, freight, gate passage, requisition. Ide Sachiko records the debt of each taking while Shinjo Boroldai counts the day a delayed dispatch will lose. Iuchi Nergui lays a household tally across the faster ferry line. The team stands harnessed, but the village cart’s owner grips the shaft. When the bells fall silent, no wheel has received lawful priority.
encounters.content:
## A road heard before it is seen

The bells are a working map. One note marks a messenger entering from the northern post road, two quick notes a remount change, a low bronze voice a freight wagon too heavy for the inner bridge, and a hard little chime a cart traveling under requisition seal. Ide Sachiko identifies the route of an arriving rider without turning her head. “A road speaks before the traveler does,” she says, and rings in three couriers for the Witnesses to hear.

The first rides a Unicorn horse and carries an Imperial packet. The second leads an exhausted village mare requisitioned by a Lion patrol. The third walks because the cart animal promised to him at the western station was taken two days earlier by a Crane grain convoy. All three journeys are lawful under one emergency order or another. Together they prove that the road is open only in the ceremonial sense.

Sachiko does not ask for ownership of the roads. She asks who will decide which journey must wait, who may take an animal or cart, who records the taking, and who restores the local capacity consumed by Imperial service.

## The Roads Reed is not one power

Court language tends to compress Roads into bridges and post stations. Sachiko divides the Reed into nine powers that may be held separately.

1. **Title:** who speaks in the Emperor's name for the road system.
2. **Route planning:** who sets ordinary routes, closures, and seasonal alternatives.
3. **Execution:** who maintains stations, ferries, bridges, remounts, and schedules.
4. **Priority:** who decides whether messengers, grain, troops, labor, or private carts move first.
5. **Requisition:** who may take animals, carts, boats, fodder, and lodging for public use.
6. **Valuation and repayment:** who records what was taken, assigns its value, and pays or credits the owner.
7. **Tolls and customs:** who may collect revenue or inspect cargo without turning inquiry into seizure.
8. **Emergency closure:** who may close a route, for how long, and what alternative must remain.
9. **Succession and review:** who continues the network if an executor is removed, absent, or compromised.

A grant that assigns only title and execution leaves the most coercive powers in the margins. A grant that gives one office priority, requisition, tolls, closure, and customs can make movement depend on obedience to a private government.

## Three Unicorn positions

### Ide Sachiko: a road must survive its bargain

Sachiko built the western relief route by joining caravan associations, village relays, remount herds, temple lodging, and emergency warrants issued by four different powers. Her accomplishment is political rather than merely logistical: people who did not trust one another accepted the same sequence because each knew what the next station had promised.

She seeks Unicorn execution of Roads beneath a Miya title for one year and one planting season. She treats a road as a promise repeated at every gate, and her questions always travel outward: what token leaves the capital, what order reaches the station, what receipt returns, and what animal remains in the household afterward. She accepts Scorpion inspection of common manifests, Dragon review of disputed tolls and requisitions, and an autumn review. She will not accept several offices issuing independent priority orders to the same station.

Sachiko's preferred concession is to shorten Unicorn tenure while leaving the remount chain intact under named local successors. Her red line is a general phrase such as “necessary transport may be taken.” She has watched those words consume three animals in succession from the same household because each officer treated the previous taking as someone else's affair.

Sachiko exerts pressure by making every proposed clause travel. She asks where it begins, which gate hears it, who has the next horse, what happens when the bridge is out, and what receipt arrives at the household that paid for the journey.

### Shinjo Boroldai: speed, security, and the right to refuse delay

Boroldai commands the riders who linked the western road after the flood. He has no appetite for toll policy and little interest in formal title. He wants one person able to clear a route when delay kills.

His riders carried dike measurements, warnings of fever, seed tallies, and orders to release grain. They also carried clan demands dressed as emergency messages. Boroldai learned that a priority system with no hierarchy merely gives the fastest horse to the highest-status petitioner standing nearby.

He proposes four ordinary priority classes: Imperial dispatch, immediate danger to life or works, scheduled relief and seed transport, and ordinary official or private movement. A Sword commander may elevate military traffic for seven days under a recorded emergency, but the order must state what other traffic is displaced. Waters may claim emergency passage for crews and materials, but not close the route after the convoy has passed. Shrines may request protected movement for displaced communities and sacred objects, but the request must specify people, destination, and duration.

Boroldai will place Unicorn riders under Miya dispatch and Seppun emergency certification. He will even accept a local provincial captain as his successor. He will not accept six offices issuing independent priority orders to the same station keeper. His red line is not outside control; it is simultaneous command.

He exerts pressure with the remount board. Every new priority moves a wooden marker and visibly delays another journey. Everything can be preserved only by inventing more horses.

### Iuchi Nergui: crossings, households, and routes that are more than lines

Nergui supervised the western ferries and temporary bridges. She knows which crossings are engineering works, which depend on local rites, which exist only because particular households maintain boats, and which cease to be safe when floodwater changes the river's temperament.

She does not claim Shrines. She insists that Roads recognize the obligations on which a crossing rests. If a bridge replaces a ferry, the ferrymen lose both income and the duty by which their community understands itself. If a route moves around a flooded shrine, the temporary road may pass through burial ground or winter pasture. If the Crab northern channel cuts the west road, the substitute route requires two new stations, eighty additional horses, and a ford that cannot carry stone wagons during rain.

Nergui wants route decisions to include a crossing record: the physical work, the community that maintains it, the ritual or seasonal condition, the burden created by relocation, and the successor if the arrangement fails. She can accept Phoenix consultation and Kaiu engineering judgment. She opposes any rule in which either office may describe the whole road question in its own vocabulary.

Her red line is a map with no households on it. Her pressure is one question: who remains at the crossing after the court’s temporary executor rides home?

## The requisition chain

A valid requisition is not permission to take whatever is useful. The road network survives only if each taking passes through a chain.

1. **Authority:** the official cites the ordinary schedule or a named emergency order.
2. **Identification:** the receipt names the animal, cart, boat, lodging, fodder, or labor taken.
3. **Condition:** a witness records its condition before service.
4. **Valuation:** the schedule assigns a value or a method for later valuation.
5. **Return or loss:** the receiving station records return, injury, consumption, or loss.
6. **Debtor:** Roads, Sword, Waters, Harvest, or another named office accepts the debt.
7. **Payment date:** Accounts pays, credits tax, or records a scheduled installment.
8. **Appeal:** the owner may challenge identity, condition, valuation, or nonpayment without surrendering future access to the road.

The chain is deliberately bureaucratic. The alternative is not simplicity. The alternative is a village learning that lending one horse invites every later officer to call the household already participating.

Sachiko will accept compensation partly through tax credit, replacement animals, fodder grants, or priority access to trade. Saburo warns that these forms are not interchangeable. A merchant association can survive delayed coin. A household with one remaining plow animal cannot eat a future customs exemption.

## Tolls, customs, and inspection

Sachiko accepts a public toll schedule at major repaired crossings. She prefers no toll on Imperial messages, seed rice, shrine relocation, or laborers traveling under Waters orders. Grain convoys, merchant freight, and military baggage may pay differentiated rates if the rate funds the road rather than the officeholder.

The Scorpion may inspect common manifests and compare station copies. Inspectors may detain cargo for a fixed interval when seals conflict, but they may not set the toll, reroute ordinary traffic, or convert an inquiry into permanent seizure. Judgment hears disputes. Accounts preserves the debt and revenue records. Roads keeps the traffic moving while those offices perform their narrower functions.

A road with no inspection becomes a corridor for invisible privilege. A road where inspection can stop every rival becomes a weapon. The Mandate must preserve both movement and comparison.

## Closures and the minimum open route

Every closure must state:

- the physical or military cause;
- the authority ordering it;
- the affected traffic;
- the alternative route or an explanation that none exists;
- the hour of review; and
- the person empowered to reopen the road.

Boroldai proposes a **minimum open route** rule: unless the Emperor or a Seppun-certified emergency expressly suspends it, every district must retain one route for messages, one route for food, and one route for petitions. These may be the same road. They may not all disappear into a general closure whose author is also the beneficiary.

The rule constrains the Unicorn as much as the Lion. Sachiko supports it because a network becomes legitimate when its executor is forbidden to make rescue depend on renewed bargaining.

## Road duties the Mandate can place

### Miya title, Unicorn execution, local succession

Miya holds Roads in the Emperor's name. Sachiko executes the network for one year and one planting season. Boroldai serves under Miya dispatch, common manifests go to Accounts, and two provincial successors are trained at every district station. The autumn review can shorten, extend, or localize the commission.

### Rotating execution with one dispatch law

Crane barges, Unicorn remounts, and provincial road officers execute by district or season, but all obey one priority schedule, requisition chain, and closure rule. Sachiko accepts less office if the court does not recreate three incompatible roads beneath one title.

### Roads in exchange for bounded sacrifice

The Unicorn will accept the northern-channel design cutting the present west road if Waters funds the substitute stations, provides labor for the ford, and records the transport capacity lost during construction. The exchange is not “Roads yields to Waters.” It is a priced political decision about which district waits and who restores what was consumed.

### Public relinquishment of toll privilege

At the moon-viewing, Sachiko can surrender all emergency Unicorn toll seals into Miya custody. In return, the Mandate must adopt a proclaimed toll schedule and recognize valid requisition debts. The gesture transforms apparent private profit into visible submission without pretending the network was free.

## Failure modes

- **Roads without valuation:** every journey consumes the next season's animals and carts.
- **Priority without hierarchy:** status at the station replaces law.
- **Closure without alternatives:** commanders can manufacture dependence by obstructing rivals.
- **Customs with sanction:** inspectors become road governors without receiving the title.
- **Local succession without resources:** provincial officers inherit empty stables and ceremonial seals.
- **Compensation without dates:** every taking is acknowledged and none is repaid.

## What to record

- who holds title, execution, priority, requisition, toll, closure, and review;
- the ordinary priority hierarchy and emergency variance;
- the requisition receipt, valuation, debtor, and payment schedule;
- which traffic is exempt from tolls;
- how customs inspection is bounded;
- the minimum open route for messages, food, and petitions;
- the road consequences of the chosen Waters design; and
- the names, resources, and training of local successors.

reference_links.context: Saburo tests whether requisition, valuation, repayment, and route priority remain survivable at the crossings.
Sachiko owns the durable Roads grammar of priority, dispatch, requisition, closure, valuation, and succession.
Every route clause must survive Reedwater households, crossings, seasons, and damaged infrastructure.

encounters.title: Hall of Joined Timbers
encounters.summary: A polished beam bears nothing; broken timbers carry the room. Kaiu Masashige demands authority equal to the work while Reedwater’s witnesses force the court to price labor, land, sacred ground, displacement, and the district chosen to receive the water.
encounters.opening_view: Kaiu Masashige asks the commission to step onto a frame made from broken dike timbers. Iron straps pass their weight through the ugly joints. Nearby, one flawless ceremonial beam bears only Hida Chihaya’s work-camp roster and Yasuki Kameyo’s material debts. A fresh survey line cuts seed fields, shrine ground, and three houses. Masashige taps the brace. The river tests the arithmetic, not the seal.
encounters.content:
## The beam that does not bear weight

Kaiu Masashige invites the Witnesses onto the beautiful ceremonial beam. Lacquered and sound, it lies flat on the floor and supports nothing.

Beside it, muddy timbers joined with iron straps form a low frame. Their load passes visibly from brace to brace when the Witnesses step onto it.

“That,” he says, tapping an iron strap, “is government. The weight does not care what we intended the beam to mean.”

He does not mean that ceremony is useless. He means that a title carrying no labor, materials, decision rights, or emergency chain cannot bear the weight assigned to it. The court may give Waters to anyone it likes. The river will test the joints rather than the calligraphy.

## The Waters Reed is a chain of burdens

Masashige divides Waters into eleven powers and duties.

1. **Title:** who answers publicly for the province's water system.
2. **Survey and design:** who measures, proposes alternatives, and certifies the physical consequences.
3. **Ordinary execution:** who maintains dikes, canals, ferries, gates, and drainage.
4. **Labor assessment:** who calls households, soldiers, specialists, and hired crews.
5. **Materials:** who opens quarries, fells timber, purchases rope and iron, and assigns transport.
6. **Work-site command:** who directs crews, guards camps, and changes daily sequence.
7. **Sacred consultation:** who identifies affected sites and conducts the required procedure.
8. **Relocation and compensation:** who moves households and restores land, stipends, graves, routes, and livelihoods.
9. **Emergency authority:** who may cut, breach, divert, flood, or abandon in immediate danger.
10. **Indemnity and blame:** who answers when a design fails or another office overrides it.
11. **Maintenance, succession, and review:** who remains after the emergency commission ends.

The court's most dangerous temptation is to divide these powers so thoroughly that no one can build, then call the resulting paralysis a system of checks. The second temptation is to reunite them all in one engineer and call competence sufficient accountability.

## Three Crab positions

### Kaiu Masashige: authority equal to the work

Masashige wants Waters execution for eighteen months beneath an Imperial title. He speaks in loads, sequences, failure points, and substitutions. He draws while others speak, then turns the board so the cost faces them. He will accept Phoenix consultation, Dragon review, outside audit, and provincial maintenance succession. He will not accept responsibility for a design whose labor, materials, guards, or emergency authority another office may withhold.

He does not demand the right to choose every political sacrifice. His distinction is exact. An engineer may choose how to brace a failing section, where to place crews, and which stockpile to open within the approved plan. An engineer should not alone decide which village may be flooded, which shrine community displaced, or which road cut for a generation. Those are allocations of Imperial protection.

Masashige's red line is being ordered to certify a compromise design as though it were his recommendation. If the court chooses the northern channel to preserve villages at the cost of road access and labor, he will build it and record the cost. If it chooses the eastern wall to protect the harvest at the cost of relocation, he will build that and record who chose. He will not let political authorship disappear into his technical seal.

He exerts pressure by drawing a load path through every proposal. For each duty he asks what authority, labor, material, road, guard, and deadline actually carries it.

### Hida Chihaya: camps are settlements before they are finished

Chihaya commands the Crab guards protecting quarries and temporary work camps. She knows that a camp of eight hundred laborers is not merely an engineering resource. It is food, discipline, sickness, gambling, worship, family separation, crime, and armed authority gathered beside households already exhausted by the flood.

She wants one work-site command and one law for camp discipline. Lion patrols may guard the outer roads, Crab officers may secure dangerous work, and provincial samurai may hear ordinary local complaints, but the boundaries must be written. She opposes a camp where every uniform can issue labor orders and no magistrate knows which chain owns the act.

Chihaya also demands a labor rotation that preserves planting, harvest, funerals, and household survival. She is willing to use soldiers for heavy work and to reduce civilian calls when the garrison remains large. She will accept Dragon review of punishments and Miya proclamation of camp rules.

Her red line is a quota expressed only as bodies. A district that sends one hundred laborers from two hundred households has made a different sacrifice from a district that sends one hundred from two thousand. A household already furnishing a cart, a soldier, and shrine labor cannot be counted as untouched because Waters has not yet written its own order.

Chihaya exerts pressure by reading names. When a courtier offers “three hundred men for ten days,” she asks which households lose planting, which duties those people already bear, and who brings them home.

### Yasuki Kameyo: timber, stone, rope, and debts that become policy

Kameyo procures the material that makes Masashige's drawings possible. She has contracts for mountain timber, stone from two quarries, river rope, iron fittings, barges, fodder, and winter rice for the camps. Every contract was made under emergency uncertainty. Several sellers accepted Crab guarantees because no Imperial Accounts office remained alive to sign.

Kameyo wants materials protected from diversion and the debts entered into Accounts. She is less concerned than Masashige with who executes Waters; she is more concerned that a commission receiving responsibility cannot discover its timber reassigned to bridges, its carts taken for grain, or its work rice consumed by a garrison whose own allotment was never written.

She supports common manifests and outside audit. Her preferred rule gives every stockpile a purpose, custodian, authorized alternatives, and replacement obligation. Emergency diversion remains possible, but the office taking the material inherits the debt and schedule it disrupts.

Kameyo's red line is the phrase “from available provincial stores.” In Reedwater, every store is already promised, and availability means the last official to arrive has not yet learned whose promise will be broken.

She exerts pressure by pricing amendments. A pious, strategic, or merciful change to the plan produces a new column of timber, transport, labor, and delay. The price does not make the change wrong. It prevents the court from purchasing virtue with resources assigned to someone absent.

## Two designs, neither innocent

Masashige's eastern wall and northern channel are not a false choice between efficiency and compassion. Each creates a different province.

### The eastern wall

The eastern wall can be substantially closed before the next heavy rain. It protects the main granaries and preserves the present western road. It requires fewer labor days and less timber.

It also moves two villages, Reed Bank among them, and translates the shrine community maintained by Brother Hojun. The relocated households receive higher ground but poorer fields. Their ancestral graves cannot all be moved before construction. The shortened line also directs greater flood force toward low pasture farther downstream unless a spill basin is purchased and kept empty.

### The northern channel

The northern channel preserves the two villages and leaves the shrine community near its river. It spreads water into an older course and creates more long-term capacity.

It cuts the current west road, consumes nearly twice the timber and labor, and requires a new bridge and two remount stations. Work continues into planting season. The channel crosses land claimed by three samurai households and leaves one district outside the strongest protection until the second phase is complete.

### Amendments are new designs

The court may propose walls, gates, causeways, partial channels, staged relocation, or seasonal work. Masashige will evaluate them. Every amendment must be treated as a new allocation rather than a graceful compromise between the two drawings. The resource-and-burden ledger records what changes.

An engineering plan allocates:

- immediate and future flood risk;
- labor days and the season in which they are taken;
- timber, stone, iron, rope, carts, and animals;
- roads opened, cut, delayed, or rerouted;
- villages, fields, shrines, graves, and patrol districts relocated;
- households protected first and households asked to wait;
- emergency powers made necessary by delay; and
- blame when the chosen risk arrives.

## One burden ledger

Masashige and Rei agree on a rule neither delegation expected to share: no Waters labor order should issue until the province has one ledger of household burdens.

The ledger records, by household or recognized work group:

- adult labor already called by Harvest, Waters, Roads, Sword, or Shrines;
- military service and patrol support;
- carts, animals, boats, lodging, fodder, and tools requisitioned;
- rice contributed, advanced, or withheld for seed;
- displacement, damaged land, and loss of access;
- specialist duties that cannot be replaced by an ordinary laborer;
- exemptions, substitutions, wages, tax credits, and repayment dates; and
- the next season in which another call may lawfully be made.

The ledger does not promise equal burden. Flood risk is unequal, and specialized work cannot be distributed by arithmetic alone. It forces every unequal demand to acknowledge what the household already carries.

Chihaya proposes a ceiling on consecutive service and a right to offer a qualified substitute. Rei supports both but warns that wealthy households will purchase substitutes from poorer ones unless the exchange is recorded and limited. Kameyo proposes wages for specialized and dangerous work. Tadanobu may supply soldiers for heavy labor if Sword receives credit for reduced civilian levies rather than additional authority.

## Emergency sacrifice

A flood emergency may require cutting a dike, opening a gate, abandoning a work site, diverting water into fields, or closing a road. The Mandate must decide who can make which choice.

Masashige proposes three levels.

### Site safety

The Waters executor may stop work, evacuate a camp, consume assigned material, or alter construction sequence to prevent immediate injury. These decisions require a daily record but no outside preauthorization.

### Plan-preserving emergency

The executor may reinforce, cut a temporary relief channel, or redirect crews within the approved risk map when a named trigger occurs. A second officer witnesses the act, and review follows within three days.

### Political sacrifice

Flooding an inhabited district, abandoning a protected route, destroying a shrine structure, seizing seed rice, or changing which district receives primary protection requires a titleholder or named Imperial emergency authority. If communication is impossible and delay would produce greater loss, the executor may act, but the action creates an automatic hearing, restoration debt, and personal account of the alternatives known at the time.

This distinction denies the court its favorite refuge. It cannot grant Masashige broad emergency authority and later describe every sacrifice as engineering. It also cannot force him to wait for a poem while a work camp is collapsing.

## Work camps and local law

A stable work-camp charter names:

- the work-site commander;
- the source and duration of each labor call;
- food, lodging, pay or tax credit, and medical or ritual provision;
- the line between military discipline and ordinary Judgment;
- the handling of disputes between soldiers, laborers, and local households;
- the right to report unsafe orders without desertion being presumed;
- funeral and family-notification duties;
- the date and route of return; and
- the officer who closes the camp and accounts for its stores.

Hojun asks that displaced shrine keepers travel with camps affecting their communities. Chihaya agrees if their authority over work is limited to named sacred and funerary duties. Harunori insists camp punishments and deaths enter the common record. Namika wants sealed reporting for retaliation claims. None of these provisions removes command. They make command govern something real.

## Waterworks offices the Mandate can create

### Imperial Waters title, Kaiu execution, provincial maintenance

An Imperial commissioner holds title. Masashige executes the approved design for eighteen months. The commission controls assigned labor and materials, accepts consultation and audit, and trains district maintenance officers. The autumn review may change design only with a new burden ledger.

### Emergency directorate with a hard sunset

For six months, Waters receives integrated authority over works, transport priority, assigned guards, and materials under Seppun-certified triggers. Title remains Imperial, Judgment retains petition and recusal, Accounts preserves all diversions, and every extraordinary power expires unless separately renewed after public review.

### Provincial commission with Crab contract

Local samurai and village officers hold daily Waters administration. Kaiu specialists design, supervise the dangerous phases, and certify maintenance standards under a service covenant. This preserves local authority but requires stronger material guarantees and a clear answer when provincial officers reject technical advice.

### Staged design with priced delay

The court may begin the eastern emergency wall while funding surveys and rights-of-way for a later northern channel, or begin northern works while constructing temporary protection for the exposed district. The package is viable only if the ledger states which provisional works may be abandoned, who bears duplicate cost, and what decision at autumn ends the uncertainty.

## Failure modes

- **Responsibility without labor or materials:** the executor becomes a designated future culprit.
- **Labor without a common ledger:** the same household serves every Reed until none of them function.
- **Materials without custody:** each emergency solves itself by consuming another office's plan.
- **Engineer as final political author:** displacement and sacrifice vanish inside a technical seal.
- **Consultation without deadlines:** the river becomes the only authority able to end debate.
- **Emergency authority without levels:** every convenience becomes rescue, or every rescue waits for permission.
- **Local succession without training and stores:** the Crab leave and the province inherits drawings.

## What to record

- the chosen design and rejected alternatives;
- who holds title, design, execution, labor, materials, work-site command, and review;
- the complete household burden ledger and service ceilings;
- the custody and replacement rule for every major stockpile;
- work-camp law, security, petitions, and return;
- sacred consultation and relocation obligations;
- the three levels of emergency authority;
- who may choose a political sacrifice and who reviews it;
- indemnity when another office changes the plan; and
- the trained, funded provincial maintenance succession.

Hojun identifies the shrine community, graves, rites, and successor obligations moved by the works.
Masashige owns the Waters load path through authority, design, labor, materials, safety, emergency action, and maintenance.
Tadanobu supplies soldiers, outer security, and the boundary between military assistance and added office power.
Harunori supplies review of punishments, deaths, political sacrifice, and later design changes.
Namika supplies preservation and protected reporting for manifests, stores, retaliation, and diversion.
The engineering choice redistributes land, roads, labor, sacred duties, and future risk across the province.
Waters cannot issue labor or relocation orders before cumulative household burdens are visible.

encounters.title: Guesthouse of the Bent Reed
encounters.summary: Four flood-stained cloaks wait beyond the innermost wall. Reedwater’s witnesses expose the arithmetic hidden inside honorable bargains and demand standing that survives after the court no longer needs their testimony.
encounters.opening_view: An attendant lifts one flood-stained cloak; Rei catches the hem before it leaves the mat. Brother Hojun opens a shrine register, Saburo adds toll receipts and a cracked cart pin, and Natsugawa Kenta writes two successor names beneath every Reed. Their papers face the offices that created the burdens, not the sponsors who admitted them. Rei’s tally begins tomorrow, whether or not the court has finished listening.
encounters.content:
## The court outside the court

The guesthouse lies beyond the innermost palace wall because none of its Reedwater guests possesses the status to move freely through the Emperor's court. Their distance is architectural and political. Every Great Clan delegation can reach them. They cannot reach any delegation without permission.

The four flood-stained cloaks across the new mats are therefore not a rustic gesture. Rei refused to let attendants remove the garments because the stains are the one piece of Reedwater the witnesses are permitted to place in the room without a sponsor translating it first.

Miya Shun has secured a narrow procedure. The witnesses may answer questions placed through a Miya examiner; their statements enter the working record; and a sponsoring samurai may request that a witness attend a relevant clan consultation behind a screen. They still cannot address the Emperor directly, issue demands as equals to Great Clan delegates, or claim to represent “the people” as a unified estate.

The first political task here is not to discover what Reedwater wants. Reedwater wants incompatible things. The task is to give consequence-bearing testimony standing without pretending status has vanished.

## Four witnesses, four kinds of leverage

### Rei of Reed Bank: subtract the people already absent

Rei lays duty sticks across the mat, then removes one for every adult already serving a granary, patrol, ferry, shrine, road crew, or displaced household. She leaves the ropes from two grain sheds coiled beside the tally: one shed was recovered after she cut it free during the flood; the other fed three villages downstream.

Rei has brought duty sticks, seed tallies, household registers copied before the flood, and a new ledger kept on scraps cut from relief bales. She knows which households contain children, elders, draft animals, carpenters, boatmen, wounded veterans, shrine keepers, and adults already absent on service. Her numbers are incomplete. They are more complete than any number currently assigning burdens. When a courtier calls one more levy small, she asks, “Small after which subtraction?”

Rei will accept a harsh labor levy if it is calculable, cumulative, and survivable. She opposes equal quotas among unequal villages because equal numbers can be a polite method of choosing which smaller place fails. She wants a household to know before the collector arrives:

- what is owed;
- which prior service counts;
- who may authorize a change;
- what substitution is permitted;
- when another call may occur;
- where an appeal can be heard; and
- what happens to the household while its workers are absent.

She does not ask the court to spare Reed Bank from relocation automatically. If the eastern wall protects more lives and the village must move, she wants land, water access, seed, graves, shrine obligations, road access, and the date of possession written as one package. “Higher ground” is not compensation if its fields cannot support the households placed there.

Rei's leverage is refusal of false capacity. Every clan wants her to confirm that the province can bear its preferred burden. She will confirm exactly what it can bear and name what must be surrendered to do so.

### Brother Hojun: carry the year with the shrine

Hojun lays two bell clappers beside a household calendar marked with lamp duty, ford cleaning, burial care, festival carrying, and the promises families made after earlier floods. The bells remain under water. The calendar is why replacing them would not settle the claim.

He has brought the clappers from two bells. The bells themselves remain under water. Courtiers frequently offer to replace them. “A roof can be rebuilt in a season,” Hojun says. “Who rebuilds the year?”

Hojun accepts that sacred places may be translated, combined, or even lost under necessity. He rejects the assumption that payment for a building concludes the obligation. If a community moves, the Mandate must account for its households, stipend, calendar, graves, water access, ritual objects, and authority to teach successors. If emergency work bypasses consultation, the restoration debt belongs to the office that benefited rather than to an undefined future piety.

He and Rei disagree over timing. Rei will move before the next rain if the material package is sound. Hojun may demand a delay for rites that preserve continuity. He and Kenta disagree over authority. Kenta wants local samurai to confirm shrine keepers. Hojun insists that the community's knowledge cannot be recreated by appointment alone.

Hojun's leverage is continuity. The Phoenix can bless a policy; the Crab can preserve or move a structure; only the surviving community can make the resulting institution live in Reedwater.

### Saburo of the Three Crossings: name the debtor before the wheel turns

Saburo empties requisition receipts onto the mat and sorts them first by horse, cart, boat, room, and day lost—not by the honor of the officer who took them. Sachiko's invitation gets him through the palace gate. It does not own his testimony, and he says so before the Miya examiner records his first answer.

Saburo has brought a packet of requisition receipts. Some bear Lion seals, some Crane cords, some Crab work marks, and some only the brush signature of an officer whose unit has moved. Several describe the same animal differently. None names the office that must pay. Saburo names horses before offices and dates before honor; he understands Roads from beneath the wheel.

He supports tolls at expensive repaired crossings if the schedule is public and the revenue returns to maintenance. He accepts requisition when the taking creates an enforceable debt. He opposes both practices when they are disguised as spontaneous service expected from households too low in status to demand a receipt.

Saburo distinguishes compensation forms. Tax credit helps a landed household with a future assessment. It does not replace a dead horse before planting. Priority access to trade helps an association. It does not feed an innkeeper required to lodge soldiers for a month. Replacement in kind helps only if quality and delivery are recorded.

He and Rei disagree over valuation. Saburo wants market replacement. Rei fears that market language will let large associations price every village cart beyond the tax value used when officials take it. They can support a schedule with categories, condition records, and appeal.

Saburo's leverage is continued movement. The court can order a road open. It cannot make ruined carriers, ferrymen, and stable households possess what the order assumes.

### Natsugawa Kenta: leave an office that can answer

Kenta places three surviving copies of the lost Natsugawa archive before the examiner: a patrol roster kept by a village, a tax boundary copied by Accounts, and an irrigation judgment preserved by a ferryman. His elder brother and the house originals died in the flood. The scattered copies prove that local authority once connected offices; they do not prove that Kenta can restore it by inheritance alone.

Kenta wants local samurai households preserved as Imperial vassals rather than absorbed into whichever Great Clan executes the Reeds. His courtesy is stiff because he must ask Great Clan lords to prepare for their own departure. He does not demand the restoration of every local office as though bloodline were competence; he demands a path by which local authority can become real again, and a date by which imported banners cease to be its excuse.

Kenta accepts Great Clan specialists and temporary executors. He asks that each office name provincial deputies, training, pay, records, and a date when local officers either qualify for succession or are removed through a stated process. He opposes automatic inheritance of office by surviving households; some fled, stole, or simply proved incompetent.

Kenta and Rei disagree over exemptions. Provincial samurai households have long claimed service obligations that reduce village levies in theory. Rei's records show several households contributing neither soldiers nor labor after the flood. Kenta offers to place every local household, including samurai houses, into the burden ledger according to its lawful duty. That concession costs him support among the very families he wants to preserve.

His leverage is implementation. A Great Clan commission can govern Reedwater for a season with imported people. It cannot leave behind a province unless someone local receives seals, records, resources, and an authority other offices recognize.

## They are not one delegation

The witnesses can issue a joint statement only on narrow principles.

They agree that:

- burdens must be counted cumulatively rather than office by office;
- requisitions must create named debts;
- relocation must restore a community's means of life, not merely assign new ground;
- local succession requires resources and review, not ceremonial appointment; and
- testimony must remain available after the Mandate is proclaimed.

They disagree about:

- whether Reed Bank should move for the eastern wall;
- how long sacred rites may delay emergency work;
- whether market value or assessed value should govern compensation;
- which provincial households deserve succession;
- how heavily merchants may profit from emergency scarcity;
- how much labor Reedwater can bear before the next harvest; and
- whether Great Clan execution is a necessary apprenticeship or the beginning of permanent dependency.

A patron may obtain one witness's endorsement. It cannot honestly claim all four without accepting the constraints that make their agreement difficult.

## The burden hearing

Convene a structured burden hearing if the court has been pricing offices without adding their demands together. Each office presents what it demands from Reedwater during the next year. Rei enters the demands into one ledger while the other witnesses test the assumptions.

The hearing should include:

1. **Harvest:** rice distributions, seed protection, granary labor, and tax timing.
2. **Waters:** labor days, camps, materials, relocation, and maintenance.
3. **Roads:** carts, animals, lodging, tolls, closures, and replacement.
4. **Sword:** recruits, patrol support, provisions, billeting, and checkpoint succession.
5. **Judgment:** petition routes, witness travel, record copying, and local deputies.
6. **Shrines:** ritual labor, relocated communities, stipends, and protected dates.
7. **Accounts:** taxes, debt repayment, inspection demands, and documentation.

The ledger exposes collisions rather than producing an automatic fair allocation. The same household may appear as a source of seed rice, two laborers, one cart, a patrol recruit, lodging, and shrine duty. Cancel, sequence, compensate, or openly preserve the collision.

A useful rule is **one burden, one author, one debtor, one date of release**. Shared work remains possible, but one office must own the demand rather than every beneficiary treating it as free.

## Standing that survives the audience

The witnesses distrust one magnificent hearing followed by a year of silence. They ask for five durable forms of standing.

### Receipt of proclamation

Named district witnesses receive the same official text and correction notices as officeholders. They need not depend on a collector's paraphrase.

### Access to the burden ledger

Village heads, recognized associations, shrine communities, and provincial deputies may inspect the entries affecting them and challenge duplication or mistaken identity.

### Petition without patron ownership

A clan may sponsor travel or protection, but the petition enters under the claimant's name. The sponsor cannot withdraw it merely because the testimony becomes inconvenient.

### Trigger for review

A threshold of unpaid requisitions, consecutive labor service, unfilled local offices, displaced households, or repeated emergency extensions automatically places the matter before Judgment or the autumn review.

### Return testimony

At the autumn review, Reedwater testimony is required before commissions are renewed. The court may reject it. It may not claim there was no authorized way to hear it.

These provisions do not make the witnesses legislators. They make implementation answerable to people capable of showing that its stated premises are false.

## Sponsorship and capture

Each witness needs protection to enter the court, but sponsorship creates risk.

- The **Miya** can authenticate testimony and carry it without claiming substantive agreement.
- The **Unicorn** can sponsor Saburo's travel and route evidence but benefit from his road claims.
- The **Phoenix** can protect Hojun's sacred testimony but may elevate it above other burdens.
- The **Dragon** can preserve Rei's and Kenta's documentary evidence but may turn living scarcity into a procedural problem.
- The **Crab** can demand labor testimony because bad numbers endanger the works while still preferring the answer that keeps crews full.
- The **Crane** and **Lion** can each protect witnesses in districts they relieved or secured and may quietly exclude criticism of those systems.
- The **Scorpion** can protect identities and records but make honest testimony appear secretive by association.

Use multiple sponsors, Miya custody, or a common witness charter to keep access from becoming ownership. The best protection is not a perfectly neutral patron. It is a procedure in which no patron owns the words.

## Provincial terms the witnesses can support

### Endorsement of a harsh but legible settlement

Rei will publicly support substantial labor and tax burdens if the aggregate ledger, service ceilings, seed protections, appeal, and dates of release are real. Her endorsement can blunt accusations that every limit on clan office is sentimental weakness.

### Conditional relocation covenant

Rei and Hojun can support the eastern wall if Reed Bank and the shrine community receive land, water, seed, road access, graves and rites, stipends, succession, and a date-by-date move. Their support does not erase the sacrifice. It records consent to a specified exchange.

### Road compact

Saburo will persuade the Three Crossings association to maintain service through the next rains if valid requisitions are consolidated, partial immediate replacement reaches single-animal households, and the rest becomes Accounts debt with review. Sachiko gains capacity without receiving private control of the association.

### Provincial succession compact

Kenta will recruit surviving local samurai into deputy offices under Great Clan specialists if qualification, pay, records, burden, and removal are explicit. He accepts that some households will fail. The clans accept that competence does not entitle them to inherit the province indefinitely.

### Joint refusal

If the proposed Mandate assigns ceremonial titles while leaving cumulative burdens uncounted, the four witnesses may refuse to praise it. Their refusal is not a veto. It deprives the court of the easiest story that Reedwater received harmony gratefully.

## Failure modes

- **Testimony without standing:** the court hears facts once and builds no mechanism by which later facts matter.
- **A single “voice of Reedwater”:** patrons select the witness whose suffering endorses their preferred policy.
- **Compensation without livelihood:** relocated households receive land or money but lose water, roads, seed, graves, or work.
- **Local succession by status alone:** surviving officeholders inherit the failures that preceded the flood.
- **Local succession without resources:** the clans surrender seals and keep the horses, records, stores, and trained staff.
- **A burden ledger with no remedy:** the province receives an accurate account of its destruction.
- **Patron protection as ownership:** testimony becomes another asset exchanged among delegations.

## What to record

- each witness's independent position and sponsor;
- the burdens each office demands from every district;
- collisions canceled, sequenced, compensated, or deliberately preserved;
- the valuation and repayment form for requisitions;
- the complete relocation package for every displaced community;
- provincial deputies, qualifications, resources, and removal procedures;
- who receives proclamations and corrections;
- access, petition, review-trigger, and return-testimony rights; and
- any statement the witnesses refuse to make for the court.
