encounters.title: Evening of the Chrysanthemum Moon
encounters.summary: Seven reflected moons turn seating, poems, gifts, thanks, and refusals into public memory. Ceremony can bind honor around an exact undertaking; it cannot smuggle title, release, or burden past the drafting table.
encounters.opening_view: Applause begins before the obligation is complete. White granary keys rest beneath silk beside a folded red standard; neither bears a date, release, or field recipient. Ide Sachiko separates gifts of repayment, honor, custody, and undertaking while Kitsuki Harunori marks who can witness each exchange. Seven moons wait in seven pools, and the Imperial cup remains empty. Ceremony has made the omission beautiful enough to become dangerous.
encounters.content:
## What the evening is for

The Evening of the Chrysanthemum Moon is optional. Nothing becomes law here. That is precisely why the evening is dangerous. Use it when private concessions are individually plausible but collectively fragile: a clan will surrender a power if a rival does the same, an executor will accept review if the auditor relinquishes title, or a courtier will support local succession if service is publicly remembered before authority is transferred.

The evening cannot enact a clause. It can make denial expensive, give surrender a form that does not taste like defeat, establish which promise the court remembers as first, and expose whether several private agreements can survive one another’s witnesses. It can also humiliate a delegation, enlarge a narrow concession, or burden people who were not invited to admire the bargain.

The Emperor does not attend. His place remains screened, and a single empty cup stands before it. The cup is filled only after rival powers have named what they will surrender, accept, or carry for the sake of his peace. If the evening produces only praise and claims, the cup remains empty.

## The garden and its officers

Seven shallow pools have been cut among the white stones, one for each Reed. Narrow paths allow a guest to stand beside one reflection while facing another. The court's hierarchy still determines who may approach the central pavilion and in what order. Within those boundaries, choose adjacency, sequence, the pool toward which each exchange turns, and the witnesses placed where they cannot later claim not to have understood.

Miya Shun is the formal host. He announces each act in a sentence capable of being proclaimed in Reedwater and keeps a docket of what the participants say the act means. He refuses to record applause as consent.

Isawa Etsuko governs the cups, pauses, and sacred objects. She will not permit a drowned shrine bell, a funerary tablet, or an offering intended for a kami to become a political prop without the consent of its keepers. She can make the order of service reflect actual burden rather than clan prestige alone.

Doji Masuyo and Ikoma Noritada supervise the exchange of verse from opposite theories of memory. Masuyo seeks the phrase by which a concession appears chosen and therefore graceful. Noritada seeks the sequence of facts by which it will later be remembered as obedience rather than defeat. Either can save a bargain from humiliation. Either can also make a partial truth govern the whole evening.

Ide Sachiko receives and redirects gifts. She asks who owns the object, who must carry it, who must replace it, and whether its acceptance acknowledges a debt, transfers custody, or undertakes a future duty. She is particularly alert to gifts whose beauty conceals a requisition.

Shosuro Mirei arranges masks, recitations, and short dramatic roles. She can let a delegate speak a limitation through an honored part rather than under interrogation. She can also place a rival inside an image whose audience will remember a broader promise than the words actually made.

Kitsuki Harunori stations two clerks beyond the nearest lanterns. One records the exact words. The other records what the participants said beforehand that those words would mean. The difference becomes evidence if the court later disputes whether a promise was narrowed, expanded, or invented by applause.

Seppun Tomoe controls banners, weapons, escorts, and visible acts of submission. She will not allow a clan standard to be lowered as entertainment. If a military symbol enters the ceremony, the chain of command, replacement duty, and practical consequence must already be known.

Otomo Kazetada sits behind a half-closed screen and intervenes only when an act appears to grant office by implication, release an unnamed legal party, or establish a precedent broader than the bargain. His questions are brief: *Who benefits if this is remembered imprecisely? Who is burdened without being present? What office does the applause appear to create?*

Rei, Brother Hojun, Saburo, and Natsugawa Kenta are not brought forward to praise the Great Clans. They are seated where objects and promises affecting Reedwater must pass before them. Any one of them may answer a ceremonial claim with an implementation fact: the village that must move, the household already called to labor, the shrine community that cannot be transferred by metaphor, or the office that lacks paper, horses, and rice.

## Prepare no more than three public obligations

Choose no more than three pieces of public business. A crowded evening becomes a pageant in which every delegation can later remember only the part favorable to itself.

For each proposed act, complete a ceremonial docket:

1. **Private bargain:** What has actually been offered, by whom, and in exchange for what?
2. **Public act:** What poem, gift, seat, thanks, refusal, or relinquishment will make part of that bargain visible?
3. **Service honored:** What past act is acknowledged, and when is that emergency service considered complete or transferred?
4. **Authority affected:** What power is accepted, relinquished, limited, or explicitly not granted?
5. **Scope and term:** To which office, district, resource, trigger, and duration does the promise apply?
6. **Third parties:** Whose labor, land, rice, routes, sacred duties, records, or safety will the bargain consume?
7. **Witnesses and record:** Who must hear it, and where will the exact meaning be preserved?
8. **Graceful refusal:** How may a delegate narrow, redirect, or decline without being forced to choose between humiliation and accidental consent?
9. **Operative follow-up:** What clause, side covenant, proclamation, transfer schedule, or ledger entry must follow?

Until these questions have answers, the act is not ready for moonlight. Private ambiguity is leverage. Public ambiguity is a weapon available to everyone present.

## Seating: make a relationship visible

The ceremony cannot abolish rank. It can decide which responsibilities are placed beside one another, who faces the same Reed, who is separated by an empty cushion, and which affected witness receives a clear line of sight.

Seating can make a temporary coalition visible. Placing the Lion commander beside the Crane granary steward tells the court that Sword and Harvest are being settled together. Placing the Phoenix speaker opposite the Crab engineer tells the court that sacred consultation is part of reconstruction rather than a later objection. Placing a Reedwater witness between the Roads and Waters paths tells the court that burdens will be tested where they fall.

That visibility is not permanent allegiance. A seat means, at most, that the guests have accepted one public sequence. It does not make them a bloc on every Reed, release their private conditions, or prove they support the final Mandate. Kazetada will object if a seating arrangement is described as an endorsement. Harunori will record any explicit disclaimer.

An empty place can be more useful than a crowded one. A cushion before the Harvest pool may represent the future provincial executor whose training and resources have not yet been assigned. A place before Judgment may represent the substitute magistrate required when the first recuses. The empty seat makes a missing successor visible without pretending one has already been appointed.

## Poems: give a concession a remembered boundary

A poem can name a burden, a restraint, a relationship, or the moment an emergency duty ends. It cannot safely carry an entire bargain unless metaphor is allowed to decide its scope.

Before a poem is offered, Shun asks for its plain proposition. Harunori records that proposition beside the verse. The answering delegate may:

- accept the proposition through an answering poem;
- narrow one image and therefore one part of the promise;
- redirect the honor toward the office or community that should receive it;
- answer with a condition that must be completed before the promise matures; or
- decline to answer and state that silence is not consent.

A Crane poem about white keys resting beneath a red standard can make the paired surrender of granary custody and independent military control memorable. It cannot establish the garrison allotment, the transfer schedule, or the auditor. A Phoenix poem about a road bending around old water can make sacred consultation part of the public account of reconstruction. It cannot classify every sacred site or grant a universal veto.

Masuyo often offers a line beautiful enough to hide its breadth. Noritada often answers with a line exact enough to make surrender sound like a campaign objective. Choose the preferred danger, then write the plain proposition more narrowly than either courtier’s art.

If a poem is misunderstood, the safest repair is an immediate second verse or a plain clarification before the next cup. Allowing applause to stand as interpretation gives the loudest faction custody of meaning.

## Gifts: distinguish payment, honor, custody, and duty

Every gift should be assigned one primary meaning before it is presented.

### A gift of repayment

This acknowledges a debt for rice, transport, timber, horses, medical care, or other relief. Acceptance does not grant the recipient jurisdiction. The gift should name the debtor and whether the payment closes the account or only recognizes it pending audit.

### A gift of honor

This records service in a form the recipient may carry away: a poem, a robe, a named place in a proclamation, a recovered standard fitting, or an object made from damaged Reedwater timber. It should not silently transfer an office or renew the service being honored.

### A gift of custody

Keys, seals, ledgers, banners, dispatch boxes, and shrine registers may represent the delivery of an actual instrument. The recipient, date, condition, and authority to use it must be named. Giving granary keys to the Crane as thanks is different from the Crane presenting those keys to an Imperial Harvest titleholder.

### A gift of undertaking

Horses, bridge timbers, work bells, boats, or inspection masks may symbolize a future duty. The recipient must be free to accept the duty, narrow it, redirect it to the proper office, or return the object without the court treating every refusal as disloyalty.

A gift may be redirected rather than rejected. Sachiko can receive a set of remount bells on behalf of Roads while stating that the Unicorn accept execution, not ownership of the stations. Namika can accept a mask of vigilance while declining the visible title of Accounts. Masashige can place a cracked dike timber before the Waters pool rather than accept it as a personal accusation.

Ambiguous gifts are especially dangerous when the physical burden falls elsewhere. A courtier may give fifty carts with perfect grace because fifty Reedwater households must supply the drivers and animals. The household burden ledger must be consulted before the court celebrates generosity.

## Thanks: close emergency claims without erasing service

Public thanks should identify:

- the service performed;
- the people or places protected;
- the authority under which the service will now continue or end;
- the debt, compensation, or honor still owed; and
- the date or event after which the emergency claim is considered discharged.

“Reedwater thanks the Lion for preserving order” is dangerously broad. It may be heard as provincial consent to continued command. “The Throne records that the Lion held the northern granaries until the Seppun commission and district replacement schedule took effect” preserves honor while closing the claim.

The order of thanks matters. Burdens should be named before honors. A Crab design is not praised before the relocation and labor it requires are spoken. Unicorn transport is not praised before requisitioned horses and lost carts enter the Accounts debt. Crane relief is not praised in language that converts rice already given into permanent Harvest title.

The witnesses from Reedwater may acknowledge facts. They cannot be compelled to perform gratitude. Rei may say that the Crane barges kept her district alive and still refuse a Crane claim to the granaries. Saburo may say that Lion patrols prevented looting and still demand the return of civilian storehouse keys. Their distinction strengthens the settlement because it separates service from jurisdiction.

## Refusals: preserve a lawful path after no

A graceful refusal is not a polite silence. It states what meaning cannot be accepted and leaves the court a narrower path that remains possible.

The evening recognizes five forms:

1. **Correction:** “I cannot accept that this gift conveys title; I can accept it as custody for one season.”
2. **Narrow acceptance:** “The Lion can undertake northern patrols, not command every armed force in Reedwater.”
3. **Substitution:** “The Phoenix cannot bless this route without consultation; we can examine the northern channel before dawn.”
4. **Witnessed refusal:** “The Crab will not bear failure for a dike whose labor and materials another office may withhold.”
5. **Withdrawal:** The delegate ends the public exchange and returns the question to private drafting.

A refusal becomes politically useful when it clarifies a red line without pretending the whole Mandate is impossible. Tomoe respects a commander who refuses an incoherent commission and names the chain that would be acceptable. Etsuko respects an engineer who rejects a sacred bypass and states the emergency trigger that would justify it. Namika may refuse a title while accepting a bounded inspection duty.

Cornering a delegate can still produce apparent success. A humiliated courtier may bow, accept the object, and spend the remaining days making the final instrument fail. Decide whether the bargain needs obedience, implementation, or spectacle. The three are not interchangeable.

## Witnessed concessions: create political obligation with exact edges

A witnessed concession should be stated in a form close enough to law to have boundaries and far enough from law that the Chamber must still do its work:

> Before these witnesses, we acknowledge **the service or claim**. Upon **the named condition**, we will **surrender, accept, or perform the exact act**, limited to **the office, district, resource, trigger, and term**. **The named third parties** will bear or receive **the stated burden or remedy**. Failure or dispute will pass to **the named procedure**. The promise will become operative through **the named clause, covenant, proclamation, or transfer record**.

The ceremony can witness five useful kinds of concession:

- **relinquishment:** surrendering keys, standards, checkpoints, title, exclusive custody, or a claim of precedence;
- **undertaking:** accepting execution, supply, inspection, transport, consultation, training, or replacement;
- **limitation:** publicly narrowing an emergency power, secrecy claim, requisition right, or term;
- **conditional acceptance:** agreeing once a supply covenant, labor ceiling, sacred procedure, or substitute jurisdiction exists; and
- **release:** declaring that compensation, public credit, or completed transition settles a prior political debt.

The audience is bound politically by what it witnessed, not by every inference it could draw. A promise about western road execution does not concede customs sanction. A promise to inspect Accounts does not make the Scorpion judge. A promise to lower standards does not require troops to abandon villages before replacement.

## Four public obligations that must survive the garden

### White keys beneath red standards

The Crane present civilian granary keys to the Imperial Harvest titleholder. The Lion lower their standards, accept a bounded Seppun commission, and publish the first district replacement schedule. Miya Shun names the acts in one proclamation sequence. Accounts records Crane relief debt and the declining garrison allotment. The paired ceremony lets neither clan describe the other's concession as defeat.

Change one element and the others move. If the garrison term lengthens, the supply covenant and review date change. If the Crane retain custody of seed rice, the meaning of the keys must be narrowed. If replacement is delayed, the lowering of standards may signify obedience without immediate withdrawal. If public thanks imply permanent stewardship, Kazetada will treat the evening as an attempted office grant.

### The road beside the new water

Masashige presents two marked dike timbers: one from the old line and one from the proposed channel. Sachiko places remount bells beside the timber corresponding to the route the Unicorn can sustain. Etsuko names the sacred consultations and restorations attached to each line. Rei and Hojun state which communities and obligations each design moves. Harunori records the appeal path, and Namika's inspectors undertake to preserve manifests and stockpile records.

No bilateral bargain can complete this chain. A Crab-Unicorn agreement can move stone while ignoring households. A Phoenix-Crab agreement can protect sites while leaving the road impossible. Reedwater assent without labor ceilings can become coerced consent. The public act succeeds only when design, transport, sacred procedure, burden, record, and review are all visible.

### The mask before the open ledger

Namika declines public title to Accounts and accepts a mask representing bounded inspection. Kazetada or a Miya clerk holds record custody. Harunori names the procedure for challenging inspection and for substituting a magistrate after recusal. Mirei recites the categories of information that may remain protected temporarily. Shun states when a final finding must become public and how corrections reach the villages.

The bargain changes if Accounts execution changes hands. An Imperial executor may justify broader Scorpion comparison powers than a Scorpion executor could inspect in itself. A Dragon Judgment office may provide appeal but must recuse where its own investigations supplied the evidence. Protected Phoenix or provincial witnesses require source secrecy, but final authority cannot remain permanently masked.

### The empty cushion of succession

An empty place is set before one or more Reed pools. The current clan executor places an instrument of office beside it and states the condition under which a named provincial successor, Imperial deputy, or replacement commission will receive it. Accounts assigns pay and stores; Roads assigns the route of transfer; Miya assigns proclamation and correction; the affected Reedwater witnesses state what capacity is still missing.

The act does not appoint an imaginary successor. It makes perpetual temporary rule harder to defend. If training, records, horses, rice, staff, or authority are absent, the empty cushion remains evidence that the term cannot honestly end. If the resources are assigned, the current executor's public promise makes delay costly.

## Pressure moves during play

Use these interventions when the evening becomes too easy or too isolated:

- **Kazetada** asks which office the applause appears to grant and which precedent a distant governor will cite.
- **Tomoe** stops a military honor until the corresponding act of submission or replacement is stated.
- **Shun** reduces a ceremonial meaning to one sentence a village head can repeat accurately.
- **Masuyo** offers a graceful phrase that preserves face by making the obligation slightly broader.
- **Tadanobu** accepts the burden but refuses a symbol whose sequence would make lawful command appear shameful.
- **Etsuko** identifies the community or spirit being used as scenery and asks who consented.
- **Harunori** reads back the exact words after the court has already begun applauding a stronger interpretation.
- **Namika** praises a rival for the duty the Witnesses hoped they would accept, forcing a correction, refusal, or costly silence.
- **Sachiko** identifies the carts, handlers, road time, and replacement cost hidden inside a generous gift.
- **Masashige** asks whether the person accepting blame also receives labor, materials, and emergency authority.
- **Rei, Hojun, Saburo, or Kenta** name the district, household, shrine, or office that must live under the beautiful image.

Answer by narrowing the act, adding a third legal interest, returning it to private consultation, or allowing the refusal to stand. Not every intervention must be overcome. A useful public boundary can be more valuable than false harmony.

## Running and ending the evening

A successful evening usually creates two to four witnessed obligations, one or two useful refusals, at least one exposed dependency, and a clear list of operative follow-up. More than that is possible, but the memory of the court becomes less reliable as the program grows.

For every act, record:

- the public words and object;
- the plain meaning stated before or immediately after;
- the service honored;
- the authority affected and expressly excluded;
- the condition, term, and release;
- every outside interest or office whose burden changed;
- the witnesses;
- the legal or administrative follow-up; and
- the resentment, ambiguity, or counterclaim created.

The evening ends in one of three ways.

### The cup is filled

At least two rival powers have made reciprocal, bounded obligations to the Emperor's peace, and their dependent offices have been named. Shun fills the empty cup. The court remembers the Mandate as already possessing a public moral sequence, though not yet a legal text.

### The cup remains empty

The court has praised service but nobody has surrendered, accepted review, or undertaken a burden. The event is not a procedural failure. It reveals that private bargains were less real than their courtiers claimed. The Chamber begins with fewer obligations and more accurate distrust.

### The program is broken

A delegate is humiliated, an object is rejected without repair, an affected witness contradicts the scene, or two staged bargains prove incompatible. End the ceremony rather than force a false conclusion. The break creates a public dispute that must be answered in the Chamber or the Second Audience.

Skipping the evening remains valid. Private concessions then pass directly into drafting, where they are easier to narrow and easier to retract. Skipping the evening loses an instrument for honorable relinquishment and public sequence, not access to any necessary office or conclusion.

encounters.title: Chamber of Seven Reeds
encounters.summary: Red cords expose every dependency among office, work, stores, emergency power, succession, remedy, proclamation, and the field receipt that makes a capital order real.
encounters.opening_view: One amended word pulls three red cords taut. Otomo Kazetada strips courtesy from the clause and exposes an empty office; Miya Shun leaves its route and effective hour blank. Kitsuki Harunori follows the cords into obligations the amendment would reopen. Seppun Tomoe refuses to certify the resulting command. Around them, the ten boxes beneath each Reed fill unevenly. Both complete proposals have just become drafts again.
encounters.content:
## The table that will not forgive courtesy

The Chamber of Seven Reeds occupies a room deliberately too narrow for grandeur. Each clan may send one principal, one adviser, and one clerk. The Reedwater witnesses rotate through two places at the lower end of the table. The restriction prevents a gallery from turning every correction into triumph or insult. No delegate can look backward for permission from a wall of matching colors. Here a promise must survive the sound of its own wording.

Seven lacquered tablets stand upright in a rack above the drafting table. Beneath each tablet lie nine shallow boxes. At first they appear empty. As the scribes work, each receives a slip naming one part of government: title, execution, audit, resources, ordinary emergency action, extraordinary sacrifice, succession, term, and review. A tenth strip, laid crosswise beneath all nine, names the forum for remedy.

Otomo Kazetada calls the arrangement a courtesy to the truth. Miya Shun calls it a way to discover whether a proclamation contains a government. Kitsuki Harunori calls it evidence prepared before the offense.

The change in kind should be palpable. Earlier audiences were about claims, concessions, and pressures. Here every graceful phrase must be attached to a person, a resource, a deadline, a record, a field recipient, and a consequence. The table will accept almost any allocation of provincial power. It will not conceal who commands on the first morning, who receives the order, or what happens when the capital learns that Reedwater could not obey it.

## The officers of the Chamber

### Otomo Kazetada: keeper of the Imperial purpose

Kazetada chairs the drafting. The Chamber, not Kazetada, assigns each Reed. He prevents the Mandate from reading like a treaty among powers that happen to tolerate an absent Emperor. When a clause begins with a clan’s service rather than an Imperial need, he places a blank slip over the clan name and asks whether the sentence still commands anything.

He is most severe about recitals that flatter a coalition into authorship. The clans may be thanked. Their emergency service may be named exactly. Their concessions may be preserved in the record. The Mandate itself must remain an order issued because the Emperor governs Reedwater, not a compact that binds him because enough delegations signed it.

Kazetada's pressure is subtraction. When a clause grows elaborate, he removes every honorific and asks whether authority, burden, and remedy remain. When a coalition claims that a phrase is essential to face, he asks which operative duty changes if the phrase is removed. If none changes, the phrase belongs in a recital or proclamation. If a duty does change, the court must stop calling it mere courtesy.

### Miya Shun: reader for distance

Shun reads each clause toward Reedwater, never toward the room. He imagines a rain-soaked village headman holding only the proclamation, one schedule, and a tired messenger. He marks names that depend on court context, deadlines counted from events no district can observe, offices whose boundaries cannot be explained aloud, and remedies that require a petitioner to reach Otosan Uchi before the harm becomes permanent.

He insists that every Reed produce a first proclamation, a transfer notice, and a correction route. A Mandate may contain technical schedules unavailable to every household, but the public order must say who may command, what burdens may be imposed, when emergency authority ends, where objections go, and which prior emergency claims are closed.

Shun's pressure is repetition. He reads the same clause first as a herald, then as an executor, then as an affected household. Each reading reveals a different ambiguity.

### Kitsuki Harunori: reader for conflict and failure

Harunori maintains the contradiction ledger. He tests self-judgment, missing substitutes, and remedies that arrive after the harm has become architecture. If the Sword executor depends on Harvest for rice, he asks who decides whether a shortage is necessity or retaliation. If Waters may flood a district and Judgment receives reports from the engineer’s own clerk, he asks whether appeal exists before or only after the sacrifice.

He places a red cord between clauses that depend upon one another. An amendment to either end requires both to be reread. By the end of drafting, the table may hold a web of cords linking grain to garrison, roads to materials, sacred consultation to emergency works, Accounts to every compensation promise, and succession to every temporary commission.

Harunori's pressure is the failed holder. For each power he asks what happens if the named official dies, refuses, lies, cannot travel, is accused, receives contradictory orders, or claims the emergency has not ended.

### Seppun Tomoe: reader for obedience

Tomoe tests whether submission changes command in the field. A lowered standard, surrendered key, returned dispatch rod, or sealed resignation has no value if officers, guards, horses, ledgers, and stores remain under an independent chain. When a surrender remains symbolic, she draws one hard line through it. “Again,” she says.

She will accept staged submission when immediate replacement would endanger Reedwater. She will not accept decorative submission followed by practical autonomy. A clan may retain execution under an Imperial commission. It may not retain the same power merely because the Mandate uses a softer noun.

Tomoe's pressure is the first conflicting order. She asks whose messenger is obeyed when a former commander and a new titleholder issue different instructions on the same morning.

### The rotating provincial chairs

Rei, Brother Hojun, Saburo, and Natsugawa Kenta take turns in two chairs marked only **burden** and **continuance**. They do not possess a veto over the Mandate. They possess standing to identify a household, district, shrine community, office, or livelihood that a clause consumes without naming.

The burden chair asks who pays in rice, labor, land, danger, delay, or silence. The continuance chair asks whether the named successor has people, records, stores, routes, training, and lawful recognition sufficient to act.

A clan adviser may challenge the relevance of provincial testimony. Harunori decides whether the testimony bears on an operative consequence. Kazetada decides whether it belongs in the Mandate, a schedule, a covenant, a proclamation, or the record of reasons. The witnesses cannot simply be thanked and dismissed once their facts become inconvenient.

## Five documents, one chain of provincial command

The Chamber separates five instruments that courtiers often try to compress into one beautiful sheet.

1. **The Mandate:** the operative Imperial assignment of powers, duties, limits, succession, term, and review.
2. **The recitals:** the stated disaster, governing purpose, services already rendered, public relinquishments, and reasons for unusual divisions of authority.
3. **The schedules:** districts, stores, routes, work phases, transfer dates, review dates, named deputies, and other details expected to change without rewriting the entire Mandate.
4. **The side covenants:** supply, repayment, training, custody, compensation, and other reciprocal duties whose breach triggers a remedy but does not automatically transfer the central title.
5. **The proclamations and registers:** what households, officers, shrine communities, merchants, and local magistrates must be told; how corrections, burdens, exemptions, and claims are recorded.

The distinction is not decorative. A recital preserves honor and interpretation but does not command an officer. A schedule may be amended by the authority named in the Mandate, while the central allocation remains intact. A covenant can make military readiness reliable without giving Sword control of Harvest. A proclamation can make a lawful order intelligible without reproducing every legal qualification.

Any bargain imported from the moon-viewing must be assigned to one or more of these instruments. If no one can say where it belongs, the promise is politically real but administratively unplaced.

## The ten-part clause test

Complete ten fields for each Reed.

### 1. Imperial title

Who answers publicly to the Throne for the office? Title may carry appointment, dismissal, and the duty to report without carrying daily execution. If title is joint or rotating, the Mandate must say who speaks when the holders disagree.

### 2. Ordinary execution

Who performs the daily work and gives routine orders? Execution may be divided by district, function, season, or project. A division must name the boundary and the forum for disputes at that boundary.

### 3. Audit and inspection

Who may see records, compare claims, preserve evidence, issue interim warnings, and refer misconduct? These powers need not all belong to the same actor. Final sanction should not hide inside access or secret reporting.

### 4. Resources

Which stores, taxes, customs, labor quotas, vehicles, animals, specialists, stipends, and records are assigned? Authority without resources is an invitation to requisition outside the Mandate. Resources without a duty are a private treasury.

### 5. Ordinary emergency action

What may an executor do immediately to preserve life, records, stores, routes, or the approved plan? The trigger, duration, notice, and retrospective record must be named.

### 6. Extraordinary sacrifice

Who may flood a district, close a road for a season, divert seed rice, impose a general muster, move a shrine community, or suspend an ordinary appeal? This power should be narrower, more visible, and more reviewable than site safety or routine emergency action.

### 7. Ordinary succession

Who inherits the office after death, expiration, promotion, or ordinary replacement? What training, records, seals, and resources pass with it?

### 8. Failure succession

Who acts during accusation, recusal, refusal, incapacity, conflicting orders, disappearance, or unlawful retention? The failure successor should not depend on the disputed holder's permission.

### 9. Term and transition

When does the commission begin, mature, narrow, transfer, or end? Which conditions are calendar dates and which are capacity tests? Who certifies that a condition has been met?

### 10. Review and remedy

Who may petition, where, by what route, with what interim protection, and what remedies are available? Review may correct an act, compensate a burden, remove an officer, narrow an emergency power, or trigger failure succession. It should not be a promise that every decision will later be discussed.

## Drafting in six passes

### Pass one: purpose before beneficiaries

Write one sentence stating what the Mandate accomplishes. It may emphasize Imperial peace, survival through the next rains, reconstruction, lawful transition, or provincial restoration. The sentence will not settle every dispute, but it determines how the Emperor hears later tradeoffs.

Kazetada rejects a purpose defined as balancing clan claims. Claims are inputs. Reedwater is the governed object. The Throne's peace is the authority.

### Pass two: dangerous combinations

Before assigning names, mark combinations no single interest may safely control. Harvest, Sword, and Accounts remain the clearest. Waters design, sacrifice authority, and Judgment may be another. Roads priority, requisition, and customs intelligence may be another. Shrine classification, consultation, and final appeal may be another.

A dangerous combination may be permitted for a short emergency term, but only deliberately. If so, it must strengthen audit, failure succession, term, and first review rather than pretending the danger disappears because the holder is competent.

### Pass three: office matrices

Fill the ten fields for all Seven Reeds. Blank fields are allowed during drafting and forbidden at certification. A shared field must name a tie-breaker or escalation path. A conditional field must name who observes the condition.

This pass often exposes bargains that were never actually complete. A clan may accept execution but refuse audit. Another may accept a public title but demand resources sufficient to direct the executor. A third may offer a successor without funding the people who make succession possible.

### Pass four: cords of dependency

Harunori links every cross-office dependency. Grain supply links Harvest, Sword, Roads, Accounts, and review. Dike construction links Waters, Roads, Shrines, Judgment, Accounts, and the burden ledger. Inspection links Accounts, record custody, protected reporting, sanction, and public correction.

No amendment may be considered local merely because it changes one tablet. The cords show which other clauses, covenants, public promises, and provincial burdens must be reopened.

### Pass five: submission and first-day orders

Tomoe and Shun require an implementation packet for the first forty days. It names the visible acts of obedience, transfer of seals and records, dispatches to named field officers, receiving acknowledgments, staggered effective hours, narrow holdover duties while messages travel, replacement timetables, provisional pay and supply, and the first forums for petition.

A Mandate that begins at autumn review is not a government. Know what happens the morning after the audience.

### Pass six: read for distance, conflict, and malice

Shun reads the proclamations. Harunori assumes every officeholder will interpret ambiguity in favor of retaining power. Kazetada asks whether the instrument sounds like the Emperor's order. The provincial chairs ask whether a household can survive obedience. Tomoe asks which soldiers, guards, clerks, engineers, and messengers will receive a changed command.

Only then will the scribes certify a draft as internally complete. Certification means the instrument can be obeyed and challenged. It does not mean it is wise, merciful, or politically stable.

## Amendment discipline

The Chamber recognizes four kinds of change.

### Scribal correction

Names, dates, references, and obvious inconsistencies may be corrected without reopening assent if no power, burden, remedy, condition, or honor changes. Shun records the correction for proclamation.

### Conforming amendment

A clause may be changed to match an already accepted bargain or dependency. The affected offices are notified, but no promise is released unless its practical burden changes.

### Material amendment

A change is material if it alters title, execution, resources, emergency power, succession, term, remedy, third-party burden, or the remembered meaning of a public concession. Every dependent promise is suspended until it is reaffirmed, narrowed, replaced, or released.

### Structural amendment

A change is structural if it recombines dangerous powers, removes an outside check, changes the Imperial purpose, or makes the primary and fallback proposals cease to answer the same command. The entire affected Reed and every red-cord dependency must be reread. The Chamber may refuse to certify the draft before the audience.

Public relinquishments remain facts even when their intended clause disappears. A Lion standard lowered before witnesses cannot be made unseen by moving Sword to a different commission. The political debt created by that change must be answered, but the vanished clause does not automatically survive as law.

## Two executable provincial governments

Maintain one primary Mandate and, if needed, one fallback. Both must be complete enough to govern Reedwater. Both must begin from the same Imperial purpose. Their differences must be listed Reed by Reed, together with changed beneficiaries, burdens, submissions, resources, and first-day orders.

A fallback is not a pile of concessions removed from the primary. It is a second allocation with its own capacity and costs. Its supporters need not endorse it publicly, but the commission must know who will obey, who will obstruct, and which relinquishments remain valid.

The Chamber marks the two drafts with different seal cords. A promise attached only to the primary is tied in white. A promise attached only to the fallback is tied in black. A promise common to both is tied in gold. The colors are not shown to the Emperor as a voting map. They prevent a fallback whose implementation secretly depends on people committed only to the first draft.

Answer five questions about the fallback:

1. What failure in the primary makes the fallback preferable?
2. Which dangerous power is reduced, and which capacity is lost with it?
3. Which clan or Imperial family will obey despite receiving less?
4. Which provincial burden becomes heavier or lasts longer?
5. What must the Emperor amend if he chooses it immediately?

## Preparing acts of submission

Before the Second Audience, every intervening power should perform or schedule at least one act showing that emergency possession did not create permanent right.

Possible acts include:

- returning a granary key while retaining a written supply claim;
- lowering a field standard and accepting an Imperial commission;
- delivering a customs ledger into outside custody while preserving protected sources;
- surrendering a road checkpoint token while accepting route execution;
- sealing an emergency requisition register and opening the ordinary repayment process;
- naming the date on which a shrine commission transfers to trained local keepers;
- delivering an engineer's authority to the Imperial titleholder while retaining technical command within the approved plan; or
- presenting a roster of officers, clerks, stores, and pending orders that will pass to a successor.

Each act requires an effective time, recipient, inventory, continuing duty, and remedy for incomplete transfer. Ceremony may make the act honorable. The schedule makes it real.

## Pressure on the command chain

Closed doors do not entitle the drafters to peace.

A delegation may attempt to move a costly condition from the Mandate into a side covenant where breach appears less public. Another may insist that a recital praising service implies renewal. A technical adviser may discover that an amendment consumes labor or timber already promised elsewhere. A provincial witness may identify a household category absent from the burden ledger. A courtier may withdraw assent after learning that a rival's public concession was narrower than reported.

Useful Chamber complications include:

- the primary proposal depends on a successor who cannot act before winter;
- the fallback preserves Imperial clarity but requires twice the local labor;
- the Lion supply covenant and Crane seed reserve use the same rice;
- a sacred-consultation deadline makes an emergency engineering schedule impossible unless a bypass and remedy are written;
- the Scorpion inspection procedure protects sources but delays the public correction Shun needs to stop a false tax demand;
- a Roads closure protects work crews while preventing the magistrate's circuit from reaching two districts;
- a public gift transferred custody of keys whose underlying stores were never inventoried; or
- a clan accepts a term but rejects the person authorized to certify that the term has ended.

These are not traps with single answers. They force every amendment to reveal which promise, capacity, or burden it preserves.

## Leaving the Chamber

The Chamber produces four bundles for the final audience:

1. the primary Mandate, recitals, schedules, covenants, proclamations, and first-forty-days orders;
2. the fallback bundle, equally complete but marked by a separate cord;
3. the submission register, naming acts completed and still due; and
4. the contradiction and burden memorandum, listing risks the commission knowingly accepted.

Kazetada asks the Witnesses to sign the memorandum, not the Mandate. The Emperor authors the order; their names certify only that the court has heard its price.

Refusal does not cancel the Second Audience. It enters the record, perhaps preserving their honor after an unrecognizable amendment, perhaps convincing the Emperor that they brought advocacy rather than judgment.

encounters.summary: The final audience is dispatch, not ratification: the Emperor tests recipients, submissions, burdens, fallbacks, and the first orders that must leave before the court disperses.

encounters.content:
## One sheet beneath the throne

The seven water-darkened tablets no longer lie before the dais. In their place rests one unmarked sheet of Imperial paper, broad enough to receive the Mandate and still leave a generous margin beneath it. The margin is not decorative. It is the visible difference between advice and command.

The primary bundle lies at the Witnesses’ right. The fallback lies to the left under a different cord, with the submission register between them. Behind the Witnesses kneel the principal delegates, each bearing a full letter of authority, a named field recipient, and a courier route. They are arranged not by coalition but by the order in which present possession must become lawful service, transfer, or withdrawal.

Rei and one other Reedwater witness are present behind a low screen. They may speak only when addressed or when Kazetada certifies that a proposed amendment creates a new provincial burden not previously disclosed. Their limited place is itself a test of the Mandate's promised standing.

The Emperor does not ask for a tally of seals. He asks shorter questions than the court prefers: Who obeys first? Who pays? Who may stop the holder? What happens when the named successor is not ready? Clan approval matters as evidence of implementation, not as a vote granting the Throne authority it already possesses.

He requires the purpose of the Mandate in one sentence.

## Order before dispatch

The audience proceeds in six movements. This is not ratification by assembled interests; it is the last inspection before dispatch. Details may move, but the six movements should not, because their order determines whether submission precedes command, whether burdens have owners, and whether the first courier can leave with an order a named officer can receive.

### 1. Imperial purpose

State why Reedwater is being governed and why this distribution serves that purpose. Naming clan satisfaction, balance, or compromise as the purpose weakens the proposal. Those may be means. The Emperor expects the object to be his peace, his people, the next rains, lawful reconstruction, or the restoration of provincial government.

Kazetada then reads the first recital, including the services already rendered and the principle that emergency arrival created duties and claims for repayment, not private title.

### 2. Acts of submission

Tomoe calls each intervening power whose present possession must change. The delegate performs a completed act or presents a sealed schedule for one that cannot occur immediately without endangering Reedwater.

The Emperor distinguishes three kinds of obedience:

- **Immediate transfer:** keys, seals, standards, checkpoints, records, or command pass now.
- **Commissioned continuance:** the clan retains execution under newly named Imperial authority, limits, audit, term, and succession.
- **Staged replacement:** emergency possession narrows according to a funded schedule tied to replacement capacity.

A promise of later obedience leaves replacement unstaged. The schedule must name who performs the work meanwhile, what power has already ended, and what happens if the transfer condition is never certified.

### 3. The Seven Reeds

Present each Reed in the same order: title, execution, audit, resources, ordinary emergency action, extraordinary sacrifice, ordinary succession, failure succession, term, review, and remedy. The Emperor may interrupt after any field.

The court should not become seven repeated speeches. Each Reed is presented through its principal political danger.

- **Harvest:** Can the holder protect seed and households while feeding the garrison without turning scarcity into command?
- **Waters:** Can engineers act quickly without deciding alone which district the Empire sacrifices?
- **Roads:** Can movement and requisition remain reliable without making every passing need a permanent debt or every closure a private border?
- **Sword:** Can command remain real while belonging visibly to the Emperor and ending when its commission ends?
- **Judgment:** Can divided officers answer to one law when judges recuse, evidence is protected, and emergency acts need timely review?
- **Shrines:** Can sacred obligations survive reconstruction without allowing consultation to become an invisible veto?
- **Accounts:** Can inspection expose theft and error without letting secrecy or custody become final authority?

### 4. Dangerous combinations

The Emperor tests the links rather than the tablets. He asks who feeds the soldiers, who audits the collector, who can halt the engineer, who hears an appeal against the magistrate, who records compensated requisition, who protects a source while correcting a false public demand, and who acts when the named holder fails.

This movement often decides the audience. A proposal can sound reasonable Reed by Reed and still recreate a private province through dependencies.

### 5. First forty days and autumn review

Shun reads the first proclamations and transfer dates. Identify the first orders field officers receive, the stores and pay that support them, the petitions immediately available, and the first public evidence that emergency possession has ended or changed form.

The Emperor then asks what the autumn review can actually do. A review that can only praise or criticize is a ceremony. The Mandate should permit renewal, narrowing, replacement, compensation, correction, removal, or activation of failure succession according to named standards.

### 6. The fallback

State why a second proposal exists. It names the failure in the primary that would justify choosing the fallback and discloses the principal changed burdens. The Emperor may ask for the fallback even when the primary appears strong. He may use one clause from it as an amendment. He may also reject the premise that either draft exhausts his choices.

Maintaining a fallback is not disloyal if both drafts answer the same command. Concealing its supporters, costs, or dependence on unreaffirmed promises is.

## The Emperor's questions

The Emperor's questions are not riddles. They expose what the court has chosen to value. Use those most relevant to the proposed design.

### Questions of authorship

- Which power is held because We appoint it, and which is merely described after the clan already took it?
- What does the strongest beneficiary surrender because this is Our peace rather than its victory?
- Which recital thanks service without making service a source of title?
- If every clan denied making a bargain, which clauses would still stand as Imperial commands?

### Questions of obedience

- What order reaches the field tomorrow that did not govern yesterday?
- Which officer must obey a person of another clan, and what makes that obedience honorable and enforceable?
- What possession has already been returned?
- What remains in clan hands only because replacement is not yet safe, and who certifies that safety?
- What happens if the current holder declares the emergency unfinished?

### Questions of burden

- Which district pays most for this Mandate?
- Which households are called by more than one Reed?
- Which promise consumes rice, timber, horses, labor, or land already promised elsewhere?
- Who can petition before the burden becomes irreversible?
- What compensation is a debt, what is an exemption, and what is merely an apology?

### Questions of constraint

- Who may inspect the inspector?
- Who may judge when the judge recuses?
- Who may stop an engineer without assuming the engineer's work?
- Which secret must become public before final authority is exercised?
- Which dangerous combination remains, and why is its term short enough to be borne?

### Questions of failure

- Who acts if the titleholder dies tonight?
- Who acts if the executor is accused by the auditor?
- Which successor inherits records and resources rather than only a name?
- What order controls when two lawful messengers disagree?
- Which clause prevents the next flood from recreating seven vacancies?

### Questions of transition

- Which temporary commission ends by date, and which ends by capacity?
- Who trains the provincial successor, and what happens if training is withheld?
- What must be true at autumn review for renewal?
- Which emergency debt survives the office that created it?
- What does Reedwater govern for itself at the end of the term that it cannot govern on the first day?

## The acts of submission

The audience should include at least three visible acts, but no act should be empty theater. Select those corresponding to the actual settlement. Every act has a court instrument and a field counterpart: an authenticated order, named receiving officer, effective hour, inventory or roster, acknowledgment route, and incomplete-transfer remedy. The object before the throne changes legal claim; the matched order changes command in Reedwater.

### White keys

A Crane steward may return granary keys to an Imperial or provincial titleholder while receiving a sealed copy of the supply covenant and recognition of relief debts. The inventory must distinguish seed, household relief, military allotment, and emergency reserve. If the stores are not inventoried, the keys transfer blame more readily than custody.

### Red standards

A Lion commander may lower a field standard and receive it back beneath an Imperial commission. The recommission names the chain of command, garrison size, supply, district replacement schedule, and the date on which independent emergency command ends. Lowering without changed orders is pageantry. Recommission without lowering may look like reward for mobilization.

### Open ledger

A Scorpion custodian may deliver sealed Accounts records to outside custody while preserving a protected-source register under divided access. The act separates custody, inspection, reporting, and sanction. If final findings may remain permanently secret, the delivery merely changes the room in which authority hides.

### Road token

A Unicorn officer may return checkpoint tokens and receive route execution under a commission with bounded requisition, valuation, repayment, and closure powers. The first proclamation must tell travelers which demands are lawful and where a correction may be sought.

### Engineer's rule

A Crab engineer may lay the measuring rule before the Imperial titleholder, then receive it back for execution of an approved plan. The plan names ordinary site safety, extraordinary sacrifice, materials, labor, sacred consultation, relocation, and the official who owns political choices the engineer did not make.

### Shrine register

A Phoenix commissioner may present the register of sacred sites together with the training and transfer schedule for local keepers. The act honors the duties preserved while demonstrating that sacred expertise does not create permanent foreign custody.

### Petition cord

A Dragon magistrate may tie a separate cord to the Judgment seal, naming the substitute who acts on recusal and the route by which provincial petitioners reach review. The cord is cut only if the Mandate abandons outside appeal.

## Amendment from the throne

The Emperor may amend the proposal. His authority does not make consequences disappear. When he changes a material term, Kazetada names the dependent clauses and public promises affected; Harunori names contradictions and remedies; Shun names proclamations that must change; Tomoe names acts of submission that must be reaffirmed; the provincial witness names any new burden.

Answer an amendment in four ways:

1. **Accept and conform:** revise dependent clauses and state the cost.
2. **Accept with a narrower safeguard:** preserve the Imperial objective while limiting duration, scope, or dangerous combinations.
3. **Invoke the fallback:** show that the fallback answers the Emperor's concern with fewer contradictions or a different burden.
4. **Record an objection:** fulfill giri by explaining the predicted failure without refusing obedience.

The audience is not a contest in which contradicting the Emperor is success. Neither is silent agreement the only honorable response. The temporary office exists because the Throne asked for witnessed judgment. A precise objection may be the last service that office can render.

## Six durable outcomes

No outcome is the hidden correct Mandate. Each can govern Reedwater if its capacities and costs are honestly supplied. Use the actual clauses rather than forcing the proposal into one label.

### 1. The Imperial Spine

Imperial families hold most public titles, appeals, and failure succession. Great Clan specialists retain bounded execution under commissions, audits, fixed terms, and visible transfer schedules.

The Imperial Spine strongly restores Imperial authorship and makes mobilization less likely to create formal title. It depends on enough Imperial clerks, heralds, guards, and deputies to carry the spine. If those resources are fictitious, Great Clan executors will become the real government while Imperial title absorbs blame.

Likely supporters include Kazetada, Tomoe, Shun, clans receiving meaningful execution, and witnesses who value a clear petition route. Likely opponents are delegations asked to carry work without public status or secure renewal.

The first crisis tests whether Imperial title can issue a timely order rather than merely approve one.

### 2. Paired Custodies

The Mandate deliberately pairs rival or unlike interests: Crane Harvest with Lion supply and Sword; Crab Waters with Phoenix consultation and Dragon review; Unicorn Roads with Accounts valuation; Scorpion inspection with outside custody and Miya correction.

Paired Custodies make reciprocal relinquishment the basis of stability. It is resilient when each pair has a tie-breaker, outside remedy, and resource schedule. It becomes brittle when every action requires unanimous cooperation or when one partner can starve the other of records, rice, labor, or proclamation.

Likely supporters are factions receiving a bounded power they can defend as real. Likely opponents are those who consider shared work a public admission that a rival's claim is legitimate.

The first crisis tests whether the pairs can act before every grievance is settled.

### 3. The Reedwater Succession

Temporary clan and Imperial commissions are explicitly transitional. Provincial officers, shrine keepers, clerks, engineers, road stewards, and magistrates receive training, resources, records, and staged authority. Autumn review measures transfer rather than merely performance by outside executors.

The Reedwater Succession gives the province its strongest long-term legitimacy and reduces permanent occupation. It is the hardest to implement immediately. Local capacity is uneven, village interests conflict, and a provincial successor can become the client of whichever clan funds training and stores.

Likely supporters include Rei, Saburo, Hojun, Kenta, Shun, and delegations willing to convert emergency service into honored completion. Likely opponents are executors who distrust local capacity or expect transition conditions never to be met.

The first crisis tests whether the new local officer is allowed to fail, learn, and still retain lawful authority.

### 4. The Reconstruction Directorate

For a short and explicit term, Waters, Roads, labor coordination, materials, and selected emergency powers are joined under an Imperially titled reconstruction directorate. Harvest, Sword, Shrines, Judgment, Accounts, and provincial standing remain outside checks with strong failure succession and a hard sunset.

The Reconstruction Directorate has the greatest capacity before the next rains. It also creates the most dangerous concentration of power and burden. Its legitimacy depends on named political sacrifice authority, a cumulative burden ledger, independent records, fast appeal, and a sunset that cannot be certified solely by the directorate.

Likely supporters include engineers, logisticians, military officers concerned with timing, and courtiers who fear paralysis. Likely opponents are displaced districts, sacred communities, and anyone who believes temporary concentration in Rokugan tends to acquire descendants.

The first crisis tests whether the directorate reports a failure that would justify narrowing its own authority.

### 5. The Honored Occupation

The current emergency powers remain in place for one harvest under explicit Imperial commissions. The Mandate replaces private claims with public terms, supply, audit, compensation, submission, and a fixed demobilization sequence, but it does not attempt immediate structural transformation.

The Honored Occupation minimizes disruption and may preserve lives through the next season. It risks teaching that mobilization is rewarded so long as the resulting occupation is competently regularized. Its honor depends on visible surrender before recommission, no automatic renewal, and real replacement work beginning immediately.

Likely supporters are current executors, districts dependent on existing relief chains, and officials skeptical of untested successors. Likely opponents are Kazetada, clans excluded from present possession, and witnesses who already experience emergency burdens as permanent.

The first crisis tests whether an executor treats the Mandate as a limit or as recognition of what it had already won.

### 6. The Narrow Imperial Peace

The Emperor rejects much of the architecture and issues a narrower order: immediate military submission, temporary continuation of essential relief, a small set of divided offices, and a new commission to complete the rest after the next rains.

The Narrow Imperial Peace may prevent clan war without solving Reedwater's government. It can still be a partial success if it closes the most dangerous claims, protects seed and reconstruction, preserves provincial standing, and creates a lawful deadline for unfinished work. It becomes failure if delay merely gives temporary holders another season to entrench.

The Witnesses may lose patronage because preferred offices remain unresolved. It may also preserve the province from an elegant Mandate whose capacities were invented.

The first crisis tests whether the unfinished commission can deliberate without the emergency settlement becoming the new normal.

## Failure without collapse

The Emperor may reject the primary, choose the fallback, or impose an amendment that damages a patron. None automatically means the commission failed. Their giri was to bring a governable judgment, expose costs, and prevent emergency possession from becoming invisible law.

Conversely, adoption as written is not automatic success. A beautiful Mandate with unfunded successors, cumulative labor demands, decorative submission, or inaccessible remedies may fail in Reedwater while winning every courtly appearance.

Judge the outcome across six dimensions:

- **Authorship:** Does the settlement remain recognizably Imperial?
- **Obedience:** Have present holders changed command, custody, or legal status?
- **Capacity:** Can the named actors perform the work with assigned resources?
- **Constraint:** Can dangerous powers be inspected, stopped, appealed, and succeeded?
- **Burden legitimacy:** Are costs named, cumulative, contestable, and compensated where promised?
- **Transition:** Does the arrangement end, mature, or transfer through observable conditions?

A Mandate may be strong in four dimensions and deliberately weak in two. Record those weaknesses as future political material rather than hiding them behind a single success grade.

## Imperial issuance

After questions and amendments, the Emperor writes or dictates one of five dispositions:

- adopted substantially as presented;
- adopted with named amendments;
- primary joined to one or more fallback clauses;
- fallback adopted with amendments; or
- narrow Imperial peace issued while the larger settlement is returned for later work.

He then commands the first acts, not merely the final seals. Before the court disperses, a messenger is already running. A standard lowers, a key changes hands, an order is copied, a burden ledger is opened, and an engineer receives authority beneath a name not his own.

The final image should belong to the consequence chosen. The unmarked margin may remain small, showing that the drafted work endured. It may contain one decisive line that rearranges a coalition. It may be filled with Imperial corrections. Or the Emperor may set the broad sheet aside and write a shorter order on fresh paper.

Whatever the disposition, the seven old tablets are not returned to their places. The flood ended that government. What leaves the hall is not its restoration, but the first order of the thing that must grow after it.

## What to record

- the stated Imperial purpose;
- the primary and fallback architectures;
- acts of submission completed, scheduled, or refused;
- every amendment and the dependencies it reopened;
- the Emperor’s questions the Witnesses could not answer;
- the adopted disposition and first-forty-days orders;
- patrons honored, disappointed, or exposed;
- burdens accepted by Reedwater and remedies preserved;
- dangerous combinations knowingly retained; and
- the first political crisis implied by the chosen outcome.

reference_links.context: Kazetada tests whether the disposition remains an Imperial order rather than a settlement of clan possession.
Tomoe tests whether submission, command, removal, and the first field orders are operationally real.
Shun tests the recipients, routes, acknowledgments, corrections, and petitions that carry issuance outward.
Rei's standing keeps cumulative household burdens and relocation capacity visible at judgment.
Hojun's standing keeps displaced shrine communities and restoration obligations visible at judgment.
Saburo's standing keeps transport losses, valuation, debtors, and usable remedies visible at judgment.
Kenta's standing keeps local succession, resources, recognition, and removal visible at judgment.
The Emperor tests whether all seven office domains form one Imperial command with capacity and transition.
The final Harvest terms must distinguish service, debt, civilian execution, seed, and public credit without granting ownership by gratitude.
The final Sword terms must convert present command into bounded Imperial service or lawful withdrawal.
The final Shrines terms must preserve living obligations, emergency rules, restoration debt, and review.
The final Judgment terms must keep reasons, recusal, appeal, records, and remedy outside interested offices.
The final Accounts terms must preserve comparison and protected reporting without allowing secret self-government.
The final Roads terms must reach stations, carriers, debtors, recipients, and provincial successors.
The final Waters terms must assign design, labor, stores, emergency powers, burdens, and maintenance honestly.
The final audience asks what changes first in Reedwater rather than which delegates applaud in court.
The Emperor tests whether cumulative costs are named, contestable, receipted, and remedied.
The adopted Mandate becomes government only when submissions, field orders, recipients, effective hours, and acknowledgments leave the room.

revelations.title: Divide the power before the blame
revelations.description: Otomo Kazetada will support a complex settlement that separates title, execution, audit, and succession, especially where that prevents one Great Clan from combining military, fiscal, and food authority.

revelations.title: A clan sword may serve beneath an Imperial hand
revelations.description: Seppun Tomoe can accept Great Clan troops in Reedwater if their commander holds a revocable Imperial commission, emergency authority is bounded, and the mobilized forces perform visible obedience before receiving office.

revelations.title: An order must survive the road
revelations.description: Miya Shun will support almost any allocation whose dates, routes, transition, petitions, and correction procedure can be stated plainly to every district before local improvisation becomes law.

revelations.title: Grain is not spoil
revelations.description: Doji Masuyo can concede the Sword and accept outside audit if civilian officials control granaries, military requisition is bounded, and Crane relief receives durable public credit or compensation.

revelations.title: Command must be real before it can be bounded
revelations.description: Akodo Tadanobu can accept Imperial limits, civilian granaries, and external audit if the Sword has one legible chain of command and Lion service is concluded as honorable obedience rather than punished ambition.

revelations.title: Sacred duty must survive the work
revelations.description: Isawa Etsuko can bless and support reconstruction if sacred boundaries, ritual communities, and consultation duties survive the engineering plan and cannot be waived by the office benefiting from the waiver.

revelations.title: Divided offices need one law
revelations.description: Kitsuki Harunori can design a circuit of recusal, appeal, and retrospective review that gives divided offices a common law without allowing any officeholder to judge its own conduct.

revelations.title: Inspection does not require possession
revelations.description: Bayushi Namika can relinquish title to Accounts if Scorpion inspectors receive access to manifests, protected reporting, and independence from the officials they inspect.

revelations.title: An open road must not become a lawful taking
revelations.description: Ide Sachiko can restore transport through remounts, bridges, and caravan schedules if tolls are capped, requisitions are compensated, and local commanders cannot close roads merely to create political leverage.

revelations.title: Authority must bear the same weight as blame
revelations.description: Kaiu Masashige will execute the Waters if the office controls labor, materials, work-site security, and emergency choices and is not blamed for compromises imposed by unrelated officeholders.

revelations.title: Reedwater must remain more than testimony
revelations.description: Miya procedure and several clan sponsors can place provincial testimony in the record, but the witnesses will support the settlement only if they may speak to burdens and failures rather than merely praise their patrons.

revelations.title: Ceremony can bind memory, not enact law
revelations.description: Poems, gifts, seating, and public thanks can make a limited promise costly to retract without turning it into law; the same scene can also create humiliation or unintended obligations.

revelations.title: The Chamber can turn bargains into government
revelations.description: The Chamber of Seven Reeds can convert political bargains into clauses that separately assign public title, daily work, oversight, resources, emergency authority, succession, and review.

revelations.title: The Mandate must remain the Emperor’s act
revelations.description: The final proposal must begin from an Imperial purpose, require visible obedience from the intervening clans, and distinguish reward for service from title acquired by arriving with force.

revelations.title: Food, force, and self-certification make a private province
revelations.description: A power that can feed the province, command its troops, and certify the cost can turn temporary relief into a self-justifying private government even without openly defying the Emperor.

revelations.title: A fixed ending can make surrender honorable
revelations.description: A clan can accept yielding a permanent claim when the Mandate describes the arrangement as time-bounded service, names a public review, and preserves a path to argue from performance rather than wounded status.

revelations.title: Stable peace is built from reciprocal surrender
revelations.description: The Mandate becomes more stable when each major beneficiary publicly gives up a reinforcing power; a settlement that merely promises everyone satisfaction leaves every dangerous combination intact.

revelations.title: Supply can be guaranteed without giving soldiers the granary
revelations.description: The Sword office can receive predictable food, convoy priority, and a narrow emergency variance without holding Harvest, changing village quotas, or seizing seed rice. The formula must decline with the roster and record every excess as a debt of the military office.

revelations.title: An occupation ends by transfer, not announcement
revelations.description: Visible submission, transfer of keys and checkpoints, recommissioning of a smaller force, and named local replacements can end an emergency occupation without abandoning villages or presenting office as the reward for mobilization.

revelations.title: Honor can repay service without granting rule
revelations.description: Exact proclamation language, witnessed relinquishments, and compensation can preserve the honor and future claims created by relief while keeping gratitude outside the legal grant of Harvest or Sword.

revelations.title: Count the burden before distributing honor
revelations.description: Labor, rice, transport, materials, debt, and displacement must be assigned before the court distributes credit, or the province will pay for a harmony designed elsewhere.

revelations.title: Every office needs a lawful heir and a failure heir
revelations.description: Every Reed needs an ordinary successor and a failure successor for death, refusal, incapacity, misconduct, or conflicting orders; otherwise the next crisis recreates the vacancy that began this one.

revelations.title: A complete fallback is lawful leverage
revelations.description: A second complete proposal can make concessions credible and give the Emperor a lawful alternative, provided its supporters and costs are real and it is not concealed as a rival conspiracy.

revelations.title: Sacred consultation needs a speaker, a path, and a remedy
revelations.description: A Shrines clause becomes enforceable only when it identifies who may speak for a site or community, what consultation must contain, when emergency work may bypass it, and what restoration or review follows when the duty is overridden.

revelations.title: A recusal without a successor is a veto
revelations.description: A conflict rule must appoint the next judge, a failure substitute, a transfer deadline, and an interim order; otherwise an interested office can abolish review merely by disqualifying everyone available.

revelations.title: Inspection is four powers, not one
revelations.description: Inspectors may need access, comparison, record preservation, and protected reporting without also receiving final power to punish, remove, or rewrite the office they inspect.

revelations.title: Secrecy may shelter a witness, not the final judgment
revelations.description: Witness identities, methods, and preliminary findings may be sealed for safety, but the rules, reviewing authority, deadlines, and final disposition must enter a record capable of outside scrutiny.

revelations.title: Every taking must become a debt before it becomes a loss
revelations.description: Every taking of animals, carts, boats, lodging, fodder, or tools must identify authority, condition, value, debtor, repayment form, deadline, and appeal before public service quietly destroys the transport capacity needed for planting and recovery.

revelations.title: Count every day of service before commanding another
revelations.description: Harvest, Waters, Roads, Sword, Shrines, and other authorities must use one cumulative household burden ledger with service ceilings, substitutions, exemptions, dates of release, and appeal; otherwise each lawful order assumes the others do not exist.

revelations.title: Every engineering design chooses who bears the river
revelations.description: Every dike or channel design assigns flood risk, displacement, sacred loss, road interruption, labor, materials, and delay among districts. Engineers must state those consequences, but the authority choosing the sacrifice must remain politically visible.

revelations.title: Someone must own the choice to sacrifice a district
revelations.description: The Waters executor may preserve life and the approved plan under bounded triggers, but flooding an inhabited district, destroying a protected site, seizing seed, or abandoning a route requires named political authority, an automatic review, and a restoration debt.

revelations.title: Reedwater’s standing must outlive the court
revelations.description: Reedwater witnesses need receipt of proclamations, access to burdens affecting them, petitions not owned by patrons, objective review triggers, and required return testimony before commissions renew; one court appearance cannot make implementation answerable.

revelations.title: A public promise needs borders
revelations.description: Public obligation should name the act, authority, district, resource, condition, term, witnesses, and operative follow-up; otherwise applause can enlarge a narrow promise into a weapon available to every faction.

revelations.title: A gift must declare what it carries
revelations.description: Keys, banners, horses, masks, stores, and sacred objects create different obligations; their giver, recipient, meaning, condition, and physical burden must be explicit before acceptance is treated as political consent.

revelations.title: Seating displays a bargain; it does not found a faction
revelations.description: Adjacency, sequence, and shared ceremonial responsibility can display one cooperative bargain, but they do not create a standing bloc, release private conditions, or prove support for every Reed.

revelations.title: A graceful refusal leaves a road open
revelations.description: A useful refusal identifies the meaning or burden that cannot be accepted and offers a narrower acceptance, substitute, condition, or return to drafting; silence and humiliation produce apparent agreement without dependable implementation.

revelations.title: Thanks should close a claim
revelations.description: Exact credit can preserve honor and compensation while stating when extraordinary service ends, transfers, or becomes ordinary commissioned duty; vague gratitude can mature relief into a permanent claim of authority.

revelations.title: Every bargain has an absent payer
revelations.description: A courtly exchange is incomplete until it identifies the households, districts, offices, routes, sacred communities, records, and successors whose labor or risk changes because of it.

revelations.title: Authority, burden, remedy, and record must travel together
revelations.description: An office assignment becomes executable only when its authority, resources, cumulative burdens, petition and remedy, record custody, and public proclamation are assigned together rather than scattered across assumptions.

revelations.title: A material amendment reopens its promises
revelations.description: A change to power, resources, emergency authority, succession, term, remedy, or third-party burden must suspend and recheck every linked covenant, public concession, schedule, and implementation assumption before the draft remains coherent.

revelations.title: Submission changes hands, orders, and records
